activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: For US federal Direct Subsidized student loans, the government pays the interest while the student is in school; unsubsidized loans build interest during that time.
story:
The financial aid letter had been sitting on Sophie's desk for six days, folded into thirds, and tonight she finally typed the college's student portal password into the browser and opened it beside the paper like a translator working between two documents. The numbers were arranged in a grid that pretended to be friendly. Grants first, then work-study, then a line that said Direct Subsidized Loan, $3,500, and below it Direct Unsubsidized Loan, $2,000. She understood the amounts. She did not understand why one of them had a word attached that the other one lacked.

She typed the words into the search bar and read, chewing the inside of her cheek. The results were dry, government dry, but the sentences were short enough. On the subsidized loan, the government paid the interest while she was in school. On the unsubsidized loan, interest built during that time, quietly, the way sedimentary rock builds, layer on layer, invisible until you looked at a cliff face and saw all the years pressed into it. She sat back. Nobody had mentioned this at the financial aid night in the gymnasium, where a man in a maroon tie had spent forty minutes lambasting private loans without once saying the word subsidized.

Her phone buzzed against the desk. Conrad. He had been texting all week about State, where he'd committed, where he wanted her to come too, and every message had the same undertone of a person building a case. You could get in-state tuition, he'd written. It's basically free. It was not basically free, and she had told him so, and he had sent back a shrugging emoji that she could still picture, its tiny yellow indifference.

She opened their thread instead of replying. Their friendship had a sedimentary quality too, she thought, four years of small deposits, and she didn't want a fight to be the newest layer. But she also didn't want to spend the evening pretending the money question was simpler than it was. Her mother had said, last Sunday over dishes, "We'll figure it out," in the voice she used for things that had no figure. The subsidized loan felt like a reprieve, a door held open for four years while she walked through. The unsubsidized one felt like a door with a meter running beside it.

She called him. He picked up on the second ring, and she could hear a game show in the background, someone winning a car.

"Did you read your letter?" she asked. "The whole thing?"

"Skimmed it. Signed whatever my mom put in front of me."

"Conrad. Mine has two different loans. One's subsidized and one's unsubsidized. The subsidized one, the government pays the interest while I'm in school. The unsubsidized one builds interest the whole time."

There was a pause, the game show audience roaring at something. "So take the subsidized one."

"It's capped. There's only so much of it. The unsubsidized fills the gap."

"So don't go to a school with a gap." He said it lightly, the way he said everything, as though the gap were a pothole she could step around rather than a canyon with a loan office at the bottom. She looked at the acceptance letter pinned above her monitor, the school with the good biology program and the price tag that had made her mother leave the room when the first estimate arrived.

"That's the decision, though, isn't it," she said. "Not the loans. The loans are just the receipt." She heard herself say it and didn't entirely trust it; it sounded like something a person says when they've decided to sound decisive. She was still weighing it. The subsidized money was real and finite and gentle to her for four years, and after those four years the interest would be hers, all of it, both kinds, and she would be twenty-two and the numbers would have compound shapes she couldn't yet imagine.

"I want you here," Conrad said, and for once there was no lightness under it. "That's all. I know I keep pushing. I just, my brother left for college and never really came back, and I don't want that to be us." It was the most he'd said about his brother in two years, and she let it sit between them while the game show played on, someone answering a question about geography.

She told him she'd think about it, and she meant it, and after they hung up she pulled the paper letter back in front of the screen and read the two lines again, the one word of difference between them, and moved her cursor slowly down toward the accept button without clicking.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Hokusai's print series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, made around 1830 to 1832, actually contains 46 prints, because ten were added after the first 36 sold well.
story:
Andrew had pinned eleven watercolors to the clothesline that ran between the garage and the fence, and now he stood in the grass with the assignment sheet in his hand, reading it again though he knew it by heart. Ten artworks around a single theme, plus an artist's statement, due in three weeks. The theme was easy. He had been painting this same backyard since September, the same angle of shed and fence and the one crooked birch, in fog, in October light, at two in the morning with a flashlight, once in a downpour from under the eaves. What he could not do was choose which painting to take down.

Eliam came through the gate with two sodas and his usual loquacious greeting, something about the bus, the weather, a pigeon that had insulted him, and then he stopped talking, which for Eliam was itself a comment. "You have eleven."

"I know."

"Is she strict about the number? Ms. Weber?"

"She said ten. She underlined it." Andrew showed him the sheet, where the word ten carried a small decisive stroke beneath it, like a verdict.

Eliam walked the line slowly, hands in his pockets, the way he looked at things when he was actually thinking rather than performing thinking. He stopped at the seventh painting, the one done in the rain, where the fence had bled into a gray wash and only the birch held its shape. "That one's the best. That and the night one with the flashlight. And this fog one, actually." He laughed. "You're not making this easier for yourself."

They sat on the back steps and Andrew told him the problem honestly, which was that the eleventh painting, the one that would have to go, was the first one. September, the yard plain and ordinary, nothing technically impressive about it. But without it the others were just pictures of a backyard. With it, they were a change, a duration, a whole season passing in one place. Or he thought they were. He wasn't sure he could say that without sounding like he was explaining a magic trick.

"Wait," Eliam said. "We covered this in art history, that Japanese guy. Hokusai. He did a series called Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, made around 1830 to 1832, and it actually contains 46 prints, because ten were added after the first 36 sold well." He popped his soda. "The title just stopped being true. Nobody burned the extras."

Andrew looked at him. "That's not really the same thing."

"It's the opposite thing. But it's the same problem. The number in the title and the number of the thing fell out of alignment, and the thing won."

Ms. Weber was watering her tomatoes on the other side of the low fence, as it turned out, and had evidently been listening, because she said, without turning around, "It's still called Thirty-six Views, though. Nobody renamed it." Then she went inside, which felt less like retreat and more like leaving him alone with the contradiction on purpose.

That night Andrew sat at the picnic table with a notebook, drafting the statement he'd been avoiding. The first attempts were pompous; he wrote that the series historicized a single suburban yard, then crossed it out because he wasn't sure what he meant, then wrote it again smaller, in the margin, where it could stay provisional. What he kept circling back to was the choice itself. He could submit ten and quietly keep the September painting as something separate, a key that no one else would know they needed. Or he could walk in with eleven and a statement that admitted the overrun, and let Ms. Weber decide whether the assignment was a container or a provocation. One was safe and slightly dishonest. The other was honest and could read as arrogance, a freshman already too proud to count.

He took the question to Brenna at lunch the next day, laying out both options, and she listened with her chin on her fist. "So you're asking us to vote on whether you break a rule."

"I'm not asking for a vote."

"Good," she said, "because this shouldn't be a plebiscite. It's your name on the statement." She pulled one of his fries. "But if you do bring eleven, lead with the September one. Make it the first thing she sees. If it's arguing for itself, you don't have to."

On Sunday afternoon the light came into the yard low and yellow, the last good light before the time changed. Andrew carried the paintings back outside and hung them in order along the line, September at the far end nearest the gate, so that anyone entering would meet the plain yard first and only afterward discover what it had become. He clipped the eleventh clothespin, stepped back into the grass, and counted them once, out loud, all the way to the end.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: The standard tuning note is A above middle C at 440 hertz, formalized by the International Organization for Standardization as ISO 16.
story:
Alyssa had inherited the guitar from her uncle's garage, an instrument with a cracked pickguard and strings so old they had gone the colour of weak tea. She was sixteen and had wanted, since March, exactly one thing: to be good enough by June that Luke's band would let her play second guitar at the community centre showcase. Every afternoon she sat on an overturned milk crate beside the lawnmower and practised chords while the smell of oil and cut grass settled over her.

The problem was tuning. She had downloaded an app that showed a needle swinging across a screen, and the needle had opinions. It wanted A, the note above middle C, at exactly 440 hertz, and it would hold a green light hostage until it got that. She learned the number the way she learned bus schedules, by repetition, and she learned from a footnote in the app's settings that the standard had been written down and formalized by the International Organization for Standardization, that it even had a code, ISO 16. She said it aloud once, alone in the garage, and the words tasted official, like something stamped on the bottom of a machine.

At the first rehearsal in the community centre's back room, a dozen folding chairs arranged in a rough horseshoe, the band tuned together. The drummer's phone emitted a single steady tone and everyone bent over their instruments, twisting pegs, and Alyssa matched it and felt a small private pride. But the keyboard player, a heavyset man in his fifties everyone called Coach, kept shaking his head. He played his A and it did not agree with theirs, not by much, but enough that the chord they all struck afterward wobbled like a table on a bad floor.

The disagreement destabilized the whole room. Two people retuned to Coach, three stayed with the phone, and the song they attempted sounded like it was coming from two different rooms. Alyssa sat in the middle of it with her green-lit needle and her certainty suddenly not worth much.

Luke watched her from across the circle, and what he noticed was how still she went. He had known her since eighth grade, when she had been the girl who memorized the cafeteria's health-inspection score, and he recognized the look of someone whose facts had stopped being load-bearing. He himself tuned by ear, badly, by leaning toward whoever was loudest, which was a strategy with a certain cowardice in it but also, he thought, a certain democracy.

Afterward, in the parking lot, he asked her what the app had said. "Four forty," she told him. "It's the standard. A above middle C, four hundred and forty hertz. It's even got a designation, ISO 16, like it's a part number for the universe." She said it without mockery and without reverence, testing it.

The next week she came early and found Ms. Siddiqui, who ran the showcase, taping programs to the wall. Ms. Siddiqui had a framed piece of calligraphy above the community centre piano, an aphorism she had printed herself: "In tune is a decision, not a place." Alyssa asked her about it, and Ms. Siddiqui said only that ensembles argued about pitch the way families argued about dinner, and that the arguing was half the music. She mentioned, almost in passing, that orchestras in some cities tuned a little higher on purpose, that the phone's green light was an agreement, not a truth, and that an audience hears a band that agrees, whatever they agree on. Alyssa stood there holding her guitar case with both hands, thinking of the pawnshop on Route 9 where the guitar had almost been sold, the shop that bought from the indigent and sold to the hopeful, and how the instrument had ended up in neither category, parked in a garage with her.

On the night of the showcase, the back room hummed with cases and cables, and when the tone sounded from the phone, everyone bent toward it, including Coach. Alyssa had spent the week wondering whether to hold the standard against them or give it up, and she still had not decided; she had only decided she would decide out loud. But before she could say anything, Coach raised a hand and said the piano couldn't be retuned in time, so they would all have to come to him. Twelve people turned their pegs toward his slightly-off A, and Alyssa's needle swung left and stayed there, red, needle pointing away from four hundred and forty, while the band settled around her like water finding its level. She looked at the screen, then at Luke, and turned her peg anyway. "Closer," Coach said, and she gave it another small twist.

activity: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
knowledge_domain: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
fact: French economist Frédéric Bastiat's 1850 essay 'That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen' argued that good economics must count the effects nobody sees.
story:
Jordan had been in the guidance office twice before, once for a schedule change and once to be told, gently, that his attendance in gym was "becoming a pattern." Both visits had taken four minutes. Today he had been given a whole half hour, which was how he knew the meeting was about his future, and therefore not really about him.

"Two offers," said Mr. Gagnon, tapping a folder that contained, as far as Jordan could tell, one sheet of paper. "That's a good problem."

"It's one problem," Jordan said. "It's just shaped like two."

The window behind Mr. Gagnon looked out on the parking lot, where the banners for the spring fair had been strung between the light posts and were starting to undulate in the wind, slow and heavy, like something underwater. Jordan watched them instead of the paper. He already knew what the paper said. He'd read it enough times.

The apprenticeship was with Ricky's uncle's shop, forty hours a week starting in July, real wages, and the lead mechanic had said, in front of witnesses, that Jordan had hands. The scholarship was to a university two provinces away, renewable for four years if he kept his average up, for a degree in something he had written down as "arts, probably" because the form demanded an answer.

"Let's talk numbers," Mr. Gagnon said. "The apprenticeship is money now. The scholarship is money later. You can weigh that."

"That's what I did," Jordan said. "That's the problem. It's not the money."

"It's usually the money."

"Stefano says I should think about what I'm not choosing. He's taking an econ class." Jordan hadn't planned to say this, but the office had that effect, the clock ticking like it was being paid by the hour. "We were at the coffee place last week and he had his syllabus out. There's this thing on it. An essay by a French economist, Frédéric Bastiat, from 1850. 'That Which Is Seen, and That Which is Not Seen.' I asked him what it meant and he read me the idea, that good economics has to count the effects nobody sees."

Mr. Gagnon leaned back. His chair made a sound like a small animal. "And?"

"And I keep doing that. That's all I do now. If I take the apprenticeship, I see the shop, I see the paycheck, I see the Honda on the lift. What I don't see is the version of me with a degree. And if I go, I don't see the version of me who's good at something by Christmas. He just doesn't exist anywhere I can look at him."

"So you're saying you can't decide because you've become an economist."

"I'm saying the essay made it worse."

There was a silence in which Mr. Gagnon clearly decided not to point out that a boy who was turning an economics reading into a reason for paralysis was perhaps overqualified for the trades, or perhaps exactly suited to them. Jordan respected him for it. Subtext, his English teacher had said in the unit on novels, is just what people say without saying it, and the whole office was full of it now, leaking out of the filing cabinet and the motivational poster of a rowboat.

"Can I tell you what I see?" Mr. Gagnon said. "I've been doing this eleven years. I see kids pick the safe thing and call it practical, and kids pick the far thing and call it brave, and in both cases it's usually just whichever version of themselves they're less afraid of. You're doing something rarer. You're actually counting."

"Counting what, though. The stuff I can't count."

"That's the point of the essay, isn't it. Bastiat says count it anyway."

Jordan looked at the banners again. One had come loose at a corner and was flapping harder than the rest, catching and releasing. Endemic, Stefano had said the night before, describing the indecision of their whole grade, everyone gripped by the same thing at once, an outbreak with no clear origin. Jordan had looked it up to check he was using it right. He was. It fit. The whole spring had been like this, every conversation in every kitchen circling the same invisible fork, everyone performing certainty for everyone else. The bathos of it, when you thought about it: eighteen years of buildup, and the future came down to a half hour in an office that smelled of old coffee and a poster that said JOURNEY.

"Here's what nobody's asked me," Jordan said. "Not my dad, not Ricky, not you. Whether I actually like working on cars, or whether I like being the guy who's already good at something while the rest of you are all still deciding. Because those aren't the same thing, and I can't tell anymore."

Mr. Gagnon took off his glasses and cleaned them on his tie, which was a tie with tiny sailboats on it, and Jordan understood that this was the counsellor's version of being quiet for a while.

"I can't tell you that either," Mr. Gagnon said finally. "The essay doesn't cover it. Bastiat counts what's unseen. He doesn't say how to know which unseen thing you'd actually want." He slid the folder across the desk. "Deadline's the fifteenth. Both of them. And Jordan, the thing about counting what nobody sees is that you'll never finish the count. At some point you just pick, and the other life stays invisible forever, and that's allowed."

Jordan picked up the folder. Outside, the loose banner freed itself entirely, lifted, and carried off over the lot toward the tree line, nobody running after it.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: The US Bill Emerson Good Samaritan Food Donation Act of 1996 gives food donors limited protection from liability, which encourages stores and restaurants to donate surplus food.
story:
The apron smelled of bleach and something older, and Rebecca tied it too tight before anyone could tell her it was supposed to hang loose. Emelia had dragged her here, arguing that college applications wanted evidence of character, though Emelia's idea of character seemed to involve standing near the coffee urn looking useful. The line outside St. Bridget's already stretched past the bus shelter, and inside the soup kitchen a coordinator named Ms. Xu was assigning stations with the brisk economy of someone who had done this ten thousand times. Rebecca got the bread table.

Her first task was to carry a crate of baguettes and sourdough rounds from the back door, where a van from a restaurant down the block had just delivered them. The woman unloading the van, whose apron read Xu's Kitchen, turned out to be Ms. Xu herself, which Rebecca only understood later when the coordinator inside was the same woman, having shed the apron for a hairnet. Emelia had absconded to the dish pit within twenty minutes, escaping the awkwardness of saying hello to strangers, and Rebecca was left alone with the bread and a queue of people who mostly did not look at her.

What she noticed, once the first hour burned off, was that the bread ran out before the soup did. She had imagined surplus as the whole problem solved, crates arriving like weather, but the arithmetic was meaner than that. A man with a library book tucked under his arm asked, quietly, whether there would be more tomorrow, and she said she didn't know, and the not-knowing sat in her chest like a swallowed stone. At her old school there had been a food drive every November, cans of corn stacked into pyramids while a banner thanked everyone for their generosity. She had believed in that banner. She was beginning to suspect that the pyramid was the point, and the corn was incidental.

Two blocks away, though, there was a bakery that closed at four. She had passed it that morning on the walk from the bus, its window full of loaves marked down to half price, and at closing time she imagined the worker sweeping whatever remained into a black bin. This became her private nemesis, the thing she thought about while ladling soup: the bin, the bread, the distance of two blocks that might as well have been a border. When she mentioned it to Emelia during their break, Emelia said the owner probably worried about getting sued. "If somebody gets sick," she said, shrugging, "guess who pays." Rebecca said the bread was fine, and Emelia said fine wasn't a legal term, and that was the end of the conversation, or at least the end of Emelia's part in it.

Rebecca carried the question back inside. She had learned, in the last few hours, that Ms. Xu could be interrupted if you led with something practical, so she led with the crate count. Then she asked, as casually as she could manage, how the restaurant had decided to send its surplus over, whether it had been frightening, legally. Ms. Xu laughed, not unkindly. "You mean the Bill Emerson Good Samaritan Food Donation Act, 1996," she said. "It gives food donors limited protection from liability. That is why I can safely donate leftover bread instead of throwing it away. Most owners don't know it exists." She went back to her clipboard, having offered nothing further, which Rebecca understood was the whole lesson: look it up yourself, the clipboard said.

She looked it up that night, on her phone, cross-legged on her bed while her mother asked from the hallway whether she'd eaten. The law was exactly what Ms. Xu had said, no more and no less, and Rebecca read the actual text twice because she wanted to be sure she wasn't embroidering it into something larger. She was not by nature a reckless person; she had once returned a library book she'd already read because renewing it felt like a small theft. But she also remembered the man with the library book under his arm, and the two facts arranged themselves against each other, her caution and his question, and she found she could not make caution win.

On Saturday she went back to the bakery at ten to four, alone, having told Emelia only that she had an errand. The owner was a heavyset woman counting the till, and Rebecca stood at the counter rehearsing a speech that immediately disintegrated. What came out instead was the truth: that a soup kitchen two blocks away ran out of bread every night, that Emerson was passed in 1996 and gives food donors limited protection from liability, that she had checked, and that if the woman was worried about being sued, that worry was smaller than she thought. The woman listened with her hands flat on the counter. "Who told you that," she said, not as a question exactly, and Rebecca said a restaurant owner who already donated, and the woman said, "Ah, Mei Xu," in a tone that suggested a history Rebecca would never learn.

Nothing was settled that afternoon. The woman said she would think about it, and asked for the name of the kitchen, and wrote it on the back of a receipt with a pencil stub that kept breaking. Rebecca walked home feeling both lighter and slightly foolish, aware that she had no way of knowing whether the receipt would survive the evening, whether anything she'd said was germane to the woman's actual reasons, whatever they were. Emelia, when told, said it was cool in a voice that meant she thought Rebecca had been weird, and that she was also, faintly, impressed.

The next Thursday, at the bread table, Rebecca saw the crate before she understood it: baguettes and round loaves with a bakery's label she recognized, stacked to the brim. Ms. Xu caught her staring and raised one eyebrow, and Rebecca raised hers back, and neither of them said anything, because there was a line out the door and bread to hand out. The man with the library book came through near the end. "More tomorrow?" he asked, and this time she said, "I think so," and gave him the last sourdough round, and put the empty crate behind her where she wouldn't trip on it.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Ontario high school students must complete 40 hours of community involvement to earn the Ontario Secondary School Diploma.
story:
Gavin's mother had commandeered the kitchen table again, her tax files spread across it like a city seen from the air, so he ate his toast standing at the counter and read the text from Yasmine for the third time. "Food bank on Fairstreet. Saturday 9. Bring the form." Below it she'd sent a photo of a sheet of paper with lines for a supervisor's signature, and the phrase COMMUNITY INVOLVEMENT HOURS at the top in a font that looked borrowed from a parking ticket.

He'd told her, on Wednesday, that he didn't need the form. "It's sixty hours," he'd said. "Sixty, and it has to be finished before grade twelve even starts." Yasmine had looked at him the way she looked at people who argued with the referee after the call had already been made. "It's forty," she said. "Forty hours of community involvement, that's what you need for the Ontario Secondary School Diploma. My brother cut it to the deadline last June." He'd started to argue and then stopped, because her brother was in grade twelve and had actually filled out the form, whereas Gavin had heard the number once, from somebody, at some point, and had been carrying it around ever since like a coin from a country that no longer existed.

The morning of the shift, his mother drove him and then sat in the idling car outside the low brick building while he stood at the door with his hands in his pockets. Inside, a woman in a lanyard, Ms. Fortin, handed him a hairnet and pointed at a pallet of canned tomatoes. "Sort by date," she said. "Oldest to the front." Yasmine was already there, sleeves pushed up, working with the efficiency of someone who had done this before and found it unremarkable.

The work was simple and then it wasn't. A man came through the line with a laminated card and a tired argument about a package that had gone missing, and Ms. Fortin handled it in a low voice while Gavin stood holding a box of pasta and pretending to study the dates. He noticed that she gave the man an extra bag of rice without announcing it, sliding it in among the rest, the way you'd slip a note to someone in class.

At the break, folding boxes behind the sorting table, Yasmine peeled the label off a syrup bottle with her thumbnail. "My brother waited until the last month," she said. "He was doing his forty hours in a panic, right before graduation. He almost didn't get his diploma because of it." She flicked the label into the bin. "He kept saying he'd start earlier. He said it for four years."

Gavin thought of his uncle's garage, which he'd helped clean out two summers ago, before the house was sold. Among the obsolescent tools, the dead drills and the drawer of keys that opened nothing anymore, there had been a wall calendar from 1994 with every day crossed off in pencil, as if his uncle had believed that marking time was itself a kind of accomplishment. Gavin had asked him once why he'd kept crossing off the days long after the year was over. His uncle had said, "Because otherwise what's the calendar for." Gavin, thirteen at the time, had found this funny. He found it less funny now, holding his own blank form, which he had brought in his backpack and not yet shown to anyone.

He took it out after the shift. Ms. Fortin signed it at the front desk, printed her name under the signature, wrote 4 in the hours column, and handed it back. "Four down," she said. "Ten more Saturdays, roughly, if you want it done by spring." She said it without approval or judgment, the way a scale states a weight.

Walking out, Gavin caught himself constructing an argument, something about how the hours were really a means and not an end, how the point of the requirement couldn't be the requirement itself. He even had a word for it, dredged up from a philosophy video he'd watched at one in the morning: teleology, the study of what things are for. But standing in the parking lot, he could hear the argument collapse under him, because the man with the missing package had needed rice, and the rice had needed sorting, and the sorting had needed hands, and the hands had needed a reason to be there, and the reason, at least today, had been a line on a form. Maybe the good and the paperwork could feed each other. Maybe that was the whole arrangement. He didn't know, and he noticed that he didn't, and he decided that noticing was worth something, though he couldn't have said what.

His mother asked about it in the car. "How was it."

"Four hours," he said. "I need forty total. For the diploma. Yasmine's brother nearly didn't graduate because he left it too late." He looked at the form on his knee, at Ms. Fortin's signature drying in the light from the window. "I'm going back next Saturday."

At home he took the magnet off the fridge, the one shaped like a lobster that had been there since before he could remember, and pinned the form to the door at eye level, hours column facing out. His phone buzzed before he'd let go of the magnet. It was Yasmine: a photo of her own form on her own fridge, held up by a cartoon magnet, with the caption "beat you to it." Below that, a second message: "also we're not signed up for next Saturday, it's full. I booked us for Sunday instead."

He looked at the form on the door, four hours recorded, ten Saturdays pencilled in his head, and typed back: "Sunday works." Then he moved the lobster magnet two inches to the left, so it held down the corner that kept curling up, and went to find the good pen.

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: In France, the directly elected president appoints the prime minister, but the National Assembly can force the prime minister's government to resign by passing a censure motion.
story:
Kevin had been sitting on the courthouse steps for forty minutes when the doors opened behind him and a woman in a gray suit came out carrying a folder with a red stripe across the top.

"You're the one from Ms. Novák's class," she said, though it wasn't a question. "She said you'd be here. Waiting for the three o'clock."

He stood up too fast. "I'm supposed to observe a session for civics. She signed the form. I have it." He dug in his backpack while the woman watched, patient, one hand on the railing.

"Motion day," she said. "You picked a good one. Come inside before the bailiff locks the front doors."

The hallway smelled like floor wax and old paper. Kevin had chosen this courthouse because it was the one his father had driven past every morning for eleven years, pointing at it sometimes, saying nothing, and Kevin had never gone inside. Now the assignment had made the choice for him: observe a public proceeding, then write a comparison paper, and Ms. Novák had circled a line in his proposal draft, the one where he'd written that impeachment and a vote of no confidence were basically the same thing, and written in the margin, "Basically?"

He was still carrying the draft, folded into quarters, in his jacket pocket.

The courtroom itself was smaller than he expected. Wood paneling, a judge nobody had warned him would be so tired-looking, a row of lawyers in dark coats. Kevin slid into the back bench beside two students he half recognized, a boy named Emmanuel from his statistics class and a smaller guy, Gael, who was eating sunflower seeds out of his cupped hand like the whole proceeding was a movie.

"What are you here for?" Emmanuel whispered.

"Same as you, probably. Ms. Novák's thing."

Gael leaned across Emmanuel. "She rejected my topic. I wanted to write about vetoes. She said I was conflating systems." He said the word carefully, like he'd looked it up on the bus.

The cases were small and slow. A contract dispute. A scheduling matter. Kevin took notes without knowing what to write down, and his mind kept drifting to the draft in his pocket, to the word "basically," to the red margin ink. Around him the lawyers argued about procedure, about which rule applied, about what body had the authority to do what, and it occurred to him that everything in the room was about authority and the paths it traveled, and that he had never once thought about those paths in his paper. He'd only thought about outcomes. President removed, prime minister removed, check.

At the recess, the three of them ended up in the hallway by the water fountain. Gael was explaining something about his cousin in Lyon, how the cousin kept complaining about French politics in the family group chat, and Kevin was only half listening until Gael said, "He says it's a mess over there because nobody can figure out who's in charge. They elect the president directly, but the president picks the prime minister."

"Then the president controls everything," Kevin said.

"No, that's the thing." Gael shook out another seed. "The Assembly can bring the whole government down. They pass a censure motion and the prime minister's government has to resign. So the cousin says the prime minister answers to both of them in a way."

Kevin's hand was still on the water fountain button, water running over his fingers. In his head, the two halves of his paper slid apart and refused to sit side by side again. In a presidential system the head of government was elected separately and removed through impeachment, which was deliberately hard, a deterrent, deterrence built into the design. In a parliamentary system the legislature could just pull the plug. And France was neither, or both, a country that had taken one feature from each and welded them together, and his sentence about "basically the same thing" now looked to him like something written by someone who had never asked where the power actually came from.

He got out the folded draft right there in the hallway and flattened it against the wall. Emmanuel looked over his shoulder.

"That's a lot of red."

"I was wrong about the middle part," Kevin said. "The comparison. I treated the two systems like they shared a spine and only differed in decoration." He wrote in the margin next to Ms. Novák's "Basically?": France, directly elected president, appointed prime minister, censure motion. Then he stopped writing, because the pen was outrunning the thought. He didn't know yet what his position was, whether the French arrangement was a compromise or a confusion, whether making removal easier made a government more honest or only more fragile. He wrote that down too, at the bottom, in smaller letters: what stays uncertain.

"That's your whole paper, though," Emmanuel said. "The uncertain part. That's not allowed, is it?"

"It has to be allowed somewhere."

The bailiff leaned out of the courtroom door. "Three o'clock session, coming back in."

Gael pocketed his seeds. Kevin folded the draft once, not into quarters this time, and followed them in as the doors closed behind him with a sound like a held breath.

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: In the recapitulation, the second theme usually returns in the home key rather than the dominant, so the movement ends settled in the key where it began.
story:
Maria had named the piano bench "the interrogation bench," because that was where Mr. Vargas made her sit every Tuesday after school and account for her crimes against sonata form.

"K. 545, first movement," he said, dropping the score onto the music rack like a summons. "You will find the exposition, the development, and the recapitulation, and you will mark them, and you will not gesticulate at the page hoping I will pity you."

"I don't gesticulate."

"You conduct with the pencil. It's very dramatic. Now, listen."

He played the opening, that bright little C major theme, then made her find it again pages later. She drew her first bracket. Exposition, she wrote in the margin, and felt briefly like a detective, until she reached the middle of the movement and everything she recognized dissolved into unfamiliar material. The development, apparently, was where Mozart took the furniture apart to see what it was made of. She marked it with less confidence, and then the theme came back, tidy as a folded shirt, and she bracketed the recapitulation and sat back.

"Good," said Mr. Vargas, which from him was a parade. "Now, the second theme. Where does it first appear?"

She found it, a little singing tune in G major, and wrote "second theme" beside it with a flourish.

"Now find it in the recapitulation."

She found that too, and here the trouble began, because the tune was the same tune, the notes wore the same faces, but something had shifted underneath it. She played the two versions back to back, slowly, one finger at a time, like a cashier comparing two twenty-dollar bills and starting to suspect one of them. The first one lifted, the second one didn't. It wasn't wrong, exactly. It was the same sentence said with a different weight on it.

"It's lower," she said. "Or it's, like, planted differently."

"Planted," repeated Mr. Vargas, in the tone of a man filing the word away to mock her with later. "Where exactly?"

She counted along, humming, tapping the pencil against her knee. The exposition version ended on a note that pointed away from home, upward, outward, demanding something. The recapitulation version ended settled, grounded, finished in the key the whole movement had started in. She stared at the two measures as if they had been switched when she wasn't looking.

"Wait," she said. "In the recapitulation, the second theme comes back in the home key. Not the, the other one. The dominant."

"The dominant," agreed Mr. Vargas. "First time through, it goes there. Second time through, no."

"So it's the same tune but it ends where it started. In C."

"You sound disappointed."

"I sound suspicious. It's a contrivance. He brings it back just so it can land in C instead of G? It's like when my dad reroutes a road trip so we end up at his favorite diner and calls it a coincidence."

Mr. Vargas played the two versions again, back to back, and let the room go quiet after the second one. Even Maria, who could be intransigent about Mozart's motives, had to admit the landing felt different. The first ending leaned forward, the second one closed like a door.

The bell rang down the hall, and Christina put her head in the door of the music room. "Are you still being held hostage?"

"I'm being deposed," said Maria. "Did you know Mozart does the second theme in the home key the second time? On purpose?"

"Every composer I've ever met does that," said Christina, who had met none.

"You're thinking of the other Mozart," said Maria, and closed the score. The bracket she'd drawn around the recapitulation was crooked, and she redrew it straight, and underneath it, small, she wrote "same tune, home key," so that whoever opened the score next would find the clue she had almost missed. Then she slid off the bench, and Mr. Vargas was already pulling out the next movement.

"Slow one," he said. "This week. And no conducting with the pencil."

Maria picked up the pencil and conducted with it anyway, all the way out the door.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: In Texas v. Johnson (1989), the Supreme Court ruled 5-4 that burning the American flag as a political protest is protected symbolic speech.
story:
Claire spread the case file across her grandmother's kitchen table, weighting the printed pages with a jar of pickled okra because the window fan kept lifting them. Her grandmother's house smelled of coffee and cedar, and outside the cicadas ran their long afternoon argument, which seemed appropriate, since Claire had two days to learn how to argue both sides of Texas v. Johnson before her college's incoming-freshman moot court showcase.

She had asked for the assignment, in a way. Deborah had wanted the flag burning side immediately, saying it was the glamorous one, the one with the easy applause, and Claire had shrugged and said she'd take whichever was left. What was left was arguing for the state of Texas, against the idea that a man could set fire to a flag outside the 1984 Republican convention and call it speech. Then Ms. Islam, the upperclassman coaching the showcase, had told them the real work was arguing both sides, that they would flip a coin on stage. Claire had nodded as though this were a normal thing to be able to do.

The problem revealed itself by the second hour. When she drafted the argument for Texas, she wrote about order and dignity and the flag as a unique symbol, and every sentence sounded like something she could believe. When she drafted the argument for Johnson, she wrote about political protest and the marketplace of ideas, and every sentence also sounded like something she could believe. She read both drafts aloud in the empty kitchen and heard her own voice taking two positions with equal sincerity, and it unsettled her, like discovering she had two reflections.

Her grandmother came in from the garden with tomatoes in her shirt hem and asked what all the paper was for. Claire explained the case, and the showcase, and the coin flip. "You have to be able to argue it either way," she said. "That's the whole point, apparently."

Her grandmother set the tomatoes down slowly. "In my day we called that saying what you're paid to say."

"That's not it," Claire said, and then, because she wasn't sure it wasn't it, she pulled the case summary toward her. "It's not making things up. It's finding the strongest thing that can honestly be said for each side. Did you know the vote was five to four? The Supreme Court, 1989. They ruled that burning the flag as political protest is protected symbolic speech, but it wasn't unanimous. Four justices thought the other way. It came down to one person." She heard herself and stopped. "One vote," she corrected.

Her grandmother sat down across from her, not agreeing, not refusing. "So the side I'd call wrong nearly won."

"Nearly isn't a side," Claire said, but the sentence bothered her as soon as she'd said it. She looked at the margin of her draft, where she'd written 5-4 twice, circled once. Five justices thought burning a flag was speech like a pamphlet is speech; four thought a nation could set something aside as beyond burning. Neither group was stupid, and neither was unanimous about why. The subtlety, she was beginning to see, wasn't in choosing a side but in admitting how narrow the choice had been.

Deborah arrived that evening with her own stack of notes and a confidence that filled the small rooms of the house. She had found her argument: the flag belongs to everyone, so no one gets to burn it. She delivered it at the counter while Claire's grandmother poured iced tea, and Claire found herself, to her own surprise, objecting. "The dissent doesn't say nobody can burn it," she said. "It says the government can regulate conduct that happens to carry a message. That's the actual fight, whether conduct can be speech." Deborah frowned at her notes. "You're supposed to be on my side half the time anyway," she said. "Yes," Claire said, "but you have to be on its real side, not a made-up one." They argued through dinner, and somewhere between the okra and the cobbler Deborah crossed out three of her own talking points and wrote, in the margin, conduct vs. speech, underline, question mark.

Later, in the guest room with its sedimentary layers of family furniture, old desk atop older dresser, Claire read the dissents until the words stopped being positions and became five and four individual justices reasoning in the dark toward a line none of them could see. She did not resolve them. She wrote at the bottom of both drafts, same words on each: five to four, 1989, and this is close, and then she underlined the second part, because whatever else the coin flip decided, that was what she wanted the audience to carry out of the room with them.

At the showcase the next morning, Ms. Islam held up the coin. "Ms. Claire. Call it in the air." The coin went up, flashing under the fluorescent lights, and Claire heard herself say, before she knew which side she'd be handed, "Whichever it is, I'm going to tell them about the fourth vote."

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: Five US states, Alaska, Delaware, Montana, New Hampshire and Oregon, have no statewide sales tax.
story:
The paystub sat open on his screen, and Austin had read it three times before it began to mean anything. Two weeks of bagging groceries at Fischer's, sixty-two hours, and the number at the top said 682.00 while the number at the bottom, the one that had actually landed in his account, said 571.43. He knew the words for what had happened between them, or most of them. Federal income tax, state income tax, something called FICA. Still, seeing the subtraction laid out line by line felt different from knowing it in principle, the way knowing about weather is different from standing in rain.

His phone buzzed against the desk. Pascal, as usual, skipping the greeting entirely.

"So I'm getting the laptop," the message said. "The one from the link. But listen, my uncle says we should drive to Portland to buy it."

Austin typed back, "Portland's like three hours."

"Sales tax, dude. Oregon has none. Zero. You buy the thing, you pay the sticker price."

Austin leaned back. He pulled up another tab, then another, because Pascal was the kind of person who stated things with total confidence whether or not they were true. The first result surprised him. Oregon wasn't some loophole or a weird exception; it was one of five states with no statewide sales tax, listed plainly beside Alaska, Delaware, Montana and New Hampshire. He read the list twice, half transfix​ed by how orderly it looked, five names in a row like a club nobody had told him about. In Washington, where Austin had been paying 8.7 percent on everything from energy drinks to his sneakers, this felt almost personal.

"Are you sure?" he sent. "Because you told me last month that gum wasn't taxed and then we got to the register."

"That was different," Pascal wrote. "Also Annie says hi. She's here. She says you should come over."

Annie was at Pascal's kitchen table when Austin got there twenty minutes later, an hour before his shift, her own laptop open in front of her. She was working on something for Ms. Mwangi, the neighbour who had hired her to organize years of files for a small tutoring business she ran out of her house. "Receipts," Annie said, before he could ask. "Years of them. She keeps every bus pass, every box of pencils. I'm sorting what she can deduct."

"Deduct," Pascal repeated, in the tone of someone who had heard the word in a movie.

"Like, business expenses come off her income before she pays tax on it," Annie said. "She bought a printer in 2019 for the business, she doesn't pay income tax on the money she spent on the printer. Supposedly. I'm still figuring out which receipts count."

Austin pulled out his phone and showed them his paystub, the photo he'd taken the night before. "Look at this. I made six hundred and eighty-two dollars and I got five hundred and seventy-one."

Pascal leaned over, and Annie did too, and for a moment all three of them were bent over the small bright screen like people reading a map. "That's the government's cut," Pascal said. "Mine looks the same. Mine's worse, actually."

"The FICA part is Social Security," Annie said. "My mom explained it once. The income tax part is the one that gets settled when you file, though. You might get some back."

"That's the refund," Austin said slowly, because he had heard his father talk about the refund every spring, usually in a scathing voice aimed at the accountant's voicemail, and he had never once asked what the argument was actually about. His father treated tax season the way some people treated a rival sports team. Austin had absorbed the hostility without the substance.

"I still think the laptop plan is genius," Pascal said. "The laptop is eleven hundred. That's over ninety bucks in sales tax here. Gas to Portland and back is like forty. My uncle says we stop at the food carts."

"Your uncle is using you for food carts," Annie said.

"Maybe. But it's still real money." Pascal turned to Austin, wanting agreement the way he always did, and Austin found himself hesitating, which surprised him. Ninety dollars was three shifts of his life, rendered and removed. And yet something about the plan bothered him, an encumbrance he couldn't name at first. Then he got closer to it. He hadn't known, until last night, that any of this worked the way it worked. He hadn't known what FICA was, or that five whole states skipped sales tax, or that a printer could be subtracted from a person's income. He had opinions about all of it anyway, inherited ones, mostly his father's.

"Go," he said finally. "Honestly, it's smart. But I kind of want to figure out my own numbers first. Like actually figure them out." He said it and heard how earnest it sounded, and Pascal made a small oof noise, and Annie didn't laugh at all.

"Take some of Ms. Mwangi's paperwork with you," she said, stacking a folder. "Half of it's receipts from office stores. I need to know if a coffee counts as a business expense when she buys it for a student."

"Does it?"

"I genuinely don't know. She says yes. The internet says maybe." Annie slid the folder across the table toward him, and outside a car door slammed, and Pascal was already pulling up the map to Portland with the sound off.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: In the UK, students apply to university through UCAS and can choose up to five courses, listed in no order of preference.
story:
Kaitlyn got to the coffee shop first, which was unusual, and claimed the table by the window with her laptop already open to the UCAS page. Five boxes. Five choices, listed in no order of preference, which meant the form didn't care which course she wanted most. It just wanted five, and she had seven, and the deadline was midnight.

Bella arrived with two hot chocolates and slid one across without being asked. "You look like you're deleting a person."

"I'm deleting two courses." Kaitlyn turned the screen toward her. "You apply through UCAS for the UK ones, right, and you can pick up to five courses. But they're in no order of preference. Nobody ranks them. So I can't even say which one's my first choice, because there isn't a slot for that."

"That's insane."

"It's efficient. It's one form instead of five." She pulled the screen back. "It's efficient the way surgery is efficient."

Nelly came in shaking rain off her jacket, sat down, and immediately stole a corner of Bella's muffin. "Have you decided?"

"That's why I texted you." Kaitlyn spread her printed list across the table, seven courses with their cities written beside them in pencil, because pen felt permanent and she wasn't ready for permanent. Edinburgh. Manchester. Two in London. The seventh, the one she actually read the prospectus for twice, was a small program in St Andrews with eleven students per year.

"The St Andrews one's the one you love," Bella said.

"I love all of them. That's the problem. If I loved one I'd just write it down."

Nelly leaned over the list. "Then cut the two you'd survive without. That's not complicated."

"It's tautological, is what it is. Cut the ones you can cut. Thanks, Nelly. Brilliant."

"You know what I mean."

Kaitlyn did know what she meant, and that was the irritating part. Her mother had said something similar last night, standing in the kitchen doorway with her arms folded: any of them will make you happy, you make yourself happy wherever you land. Her mother believed in Providence the way other people believed in weather, a thing you didn't argue with, you just dressed for it. Kaitlyn had nodded and gone upstairs and opened the UCAS page and felt something in her chest that she could only describe as wanting, sharply, and being told the wanting didn't matter because the form wouldn't hold it.

The clock on the coffee shop wall said 9:40. Behind the counter, the espresso machine sighed and hissed, cauterizing its own small fires, and Mr. Guo from the bookshop next door collected his usual at the register and paused at their table on his way out.

"Still deciding?" he said. He had watched her sit in his shop for three Saturdays with the same prospectus.

"Until midnight."

"Good. Deciding is underrated." He lifted his cup in something like a toast and pushed out into the rain.

Kaitlyn looked at the seven names for a long moment. Bella had once said that St Andrews was like an epigram, small and complete, and though Kaitlyn had rolled her eyes at the time, the comparison had stuck. The big London courses were essays: roomy, ambitious, full of qualifications. St Andrews said one thing and stopped.

"Okay," she said. "New approach. I'm not going to pretend the form knows what it's doing. It takes five and ranks none of them, so the ranking is mine, and it lives here." She tapped her own temple, then, because that was too smug, the margin of her printed list, where she wrote the seven courses in order, one through seven, and then crossed off six and five. Manchester stayed. One of the Londons stayed. St Andrews sat at the top of the page where nothing official would ever record it.

"You understand that's just for you," Nelly said. "The form won't know."

"The form doesn't know anything. It's a form." Kaitlyn began typing the five into the boxes, in no order, exactly as the system required, feeling both stupider and more honest than she had all week. She submitted at 10:15 with the rain still working the window and Bella reading the confirmation aloud in a news anchor's voice.

Then she folded the paper, the one with her real order on it, and put it in her wallet behind her bus pass, where it would soften and crease and she would keep it anyway.

"Eleven students per year," Nelly said. "You'd better get in."

"I might not." Kaitlyn closed the laptop and wrapped both hands around the cooling hot chocolate. "Ask me in March."

Bella raised her cup. "March."

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: The World Health Organization recommends adults eat less than 2 grams of sodium a day, which is less than 5 grams of salt, to help lower blood pressure.
story:
Simon had volunteered to run the blood pressure station at the health fair mostly because Katerina had dared him to, and now, eleven hours before the fair opened, he sat in the empty gym with a practice cuff and a manual that appeared to have been translated from Swedish by someone who hated Swedish. The cuff was capricious. Sometimes it hissed and gave him a number, and sometimes it just hissed, as though it found the whole business beneath its dignity.

"One twenty-six over eighty-two," Ana read off the display, wrist cocked like a game-show hostess. "What does that even mean?"

"It means," Simon said, with the confidence of a boy who had read the first two paragraphs of a handout, "that your heart is doing heart things, and I get a sticker."

Ana gave him the look she reserved for exactly this kind of answer. Ms. MacLeod had assigned each station a topic, and Simon's was the one nobody wanted: not the smoothie station, not the CPR dummies with their serene plastic faces, but "diet, exercise, and blood pressure," a phrase so dry it could have been used to preserve fruit. Tomorrow at ten, parents and freshmen would file past his folding table, and he was supposed to interpret a reading and explain how what people eat and how they move changes it. He had until tonight to figure out how.

Katerina flopped onto the bleachers with her phone held above her face. "Text from your mom," she said, because she and Simon's mother had formed some kind of alliance. "She says your grandfather's cabinet is, quote, a sodium crime scene. She found soup cans."

Simon took the phone. His mother had photographed six cans of soup lined up on the counter like suspects, and beneath them she had typed: "Labels say 800 mg sodium each. He has two a day. Is that bad? You're the health kid now. Answer by dinner."

"The health kid," Ana said. "That's an oxymoron. You ate a bagel off the floor yesterday."

"It was a controlled descent." Simon was already doing arithmetic on the back of the handout. The manual had a page he'd skimmed and skimmed again, a recommendation from the World Health Organization, and he circled it now with the pen he'd stolen from the smoothie station: adults should eat less than 2 grams of sodium a day. He knew from the label math that his grandfather, at two cans, was already past 1.6 grams before lunch, and that salt and sodium weren't the same thing, that the 2 grams of sodium worked out to less than 5 grams of salt overall, which sounded enormous until he learned a single teaspoon of table salt was roughly 6 grams. His grandfather was losing that particular contest before noon.

He texted his mother the numbers and then, because it felt incomplete, added: "Tell Grandpa less than 5 grams of salt a day, all day, everything included. It lowers blood pressure. I'll explain at Thanksgiving if he survives until then." She replied with a thumbs up and a photograph of his grandfather salting a tomato, which Simon chose to interpret as a period piece.

The gym had gone dark blue with evening. Ana had rolled the cuff onto her own arm again, and Katerina, who had decided the manual was a comedy, was reading the warning section aloud in a courtroom voice. Simon divided the remaining work into two piles. In one pile was the science: how a reading gave two numbers, what high ones signaled, how diet and exercise nudged them down over time, how a body left alone on a couch for years let its capacity quietly atrophy the way his Spanish had. In the other pile was the problem of his grandfather, a man who treated advice as a form of insult, and Simon understood suddenly that the two piles were the same pile. He could not tell a stranger at a folding table to change a lifetime of soup. He could only hand them the numbers, the way he'd handed his mother the numbers, and let the numbers do their slow arguing.

"So tomorrow," Ana said, "when some dad in a windbreaker asks why his reading matters, what do you actually say?"

"Less than 2 grams of sodium a day," Simon said. "It's less than 5 grams of salt. And walking helps, and I don't fully know why yet, which is what I'm going to say."

"That's your pitch? 'I don't know'?"

"It's the honest half of the pitch. The other half is the soup."

Katerina lowered her phone. "You're going to bring soup to a health fair."

"I'm going to bring cans," Simon said, "with the labels turned out, and a marker, and a sign that says DO THE MATH." He was already packing the cuff, which hissed at him one last time on the way into the case, and outside the gym doors the hallway lights were clicking off section by section, all the way to the parking lot.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex, published in 1949, contains the line usually translated as 'one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman', arguing that society shapes womanhood.
story:
I did not, as Ronan would later claim, hide behind the philosophy section because I was afraid of the book club. I was browsing. There is a difference, and it matters, and I will defend it to anyone except Ronan, who saw me there for twenty minutes with the same Penguin classic in my hand.

The club met in the back of Mr. Malik's shop, between the smell of old paper and the space heater he claimed was a fire hazard he refused to replace. We were six that Tuesday: me, Ronan, Tom, two women from the university, and Mr. Malik himself, who participated mostly by refilling the biscuit plate at moments of maximum tension. The book was a classic, the kind with a heroine everyone argues about, and we had reached the chapter where she chooses to marry the dull man instead of the interesting one.

"She chose him," Tom said, tapping the page. "Freely. That's the whole point of her character."

"Freely," Ronan said, in the tone he reserved for statements he considered adorable. "Tom. She lives in a world where the dull man is the only door that opens."

"That's not freedom failing, that's just the plot," Tom said. "You're calling every choice a trap."

I had an essay due on exactly this, which is why I'd come, and why I'd been browsing so intensely. The assignment wanted us to read the passage through a critical lens, feminist or Marxist, and I had spent the weekend titrating my attention between the two like a chemist who kept forgetting which beaker was which. The Marxist reading gave me the marriage as an economic arrangement, the heroine's inheritance, the dull man's estate. The feminist reading kept sliding away from me whenever I tried to hold it still.

"She wants the house," I offered. "The security. That's the Marxist bit, more or less."

"More or less," Ronan repeated, delighted, because he knew as well as I did that "more or less" was what I said when I meant "I have not finished the reading."

The older of the two university women asked whether wanting security was her want or her training. I opened my mouth to say something authoritative and instead said, with total confidence, that Beauvoir had written that women were born already made, which is, I now know, the exact opposite of the sentence. Ronan made a noise like a kettle. One of the women reached into her canvas bag and produced a fat grey book, and there it was on the page she flipped to, and she slid it across the table to me without a word, which was somehow worse than a correction.

I read it myself, out loud, slowly, so it would stick. The Second Sex, published in 1949, and the line usually translated as "one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman." Society shapes womanhood, the woman said when I finished, not as a lecture, more like handing me the other half of a sandwich. I copied the sentence onto my wrist because my notebook was in my other bag, and Mr. Malik told me that ink was bad for the skin, and I told him so was his space heater.

"Fine," I said, staring at my own handwriting. "So when she picks the dull man. Maybe the wanting itself was built in her. She was taught to want the door that opens."

"Then nothing is anyone's," Tom said. "Then my choice of biscuits is class conditioning."

"Your biscuit choices are absolutely class conditioning," Ronan said. "Nobody naturally wants the oat ones."

But Tom's joke had a real edge under it, and I felt it. If every want was trained, then what was left to call a choice? And yet the Marxist reading and this one weren't enemies, exactly. The house she wanted was money, and the wanting of the house was training, and both could be true at once, stacked like transparencies on the same page. That was my considered position, arrived at approximately forty minutes before the deadline, which is how all my positions arrive.

What stayed uncertain, and still stays, is whether the heroine would have wanted the interesting man in a different world, or whether there is no "her" underneath the wanting to ask about. I put that in the essay as a question rather than an answer, which my teacher will either admire or circle in red.

At closing time Mr. Malik stacked the chairs around us until we took the hint. Tom bought the oat biscuits on principle. Ronan walked me to the bus stop arguing that my wrist note counted as plagiarism of my future self, and I held my arm under the streetlight and read him the sentence again, and he said, "Yeah," and looked at the road, and the bus came.

activity: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
knowledge_domain: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
fact: The Collingridge dilemma, from David Collingridge's 1980 book, says a technology's effects are hard to predict when it is new, but by the time they are clear it is hard to change.
story:
The email arrived at 4:19 on a Tuesday, and by 4:24 Ashton had read it three times. The school had adopted a new system called Sentinel that would monitor students during remote assessments: webcam on, microphone on, the software flagging "suspicious behavior" for review. Ms. Gagnon had forwarded the announcement with a single line above it, "Thoughts?" which from her meant something closer to a dare.

He opened the demo video the company had posted. A cheerful voice enunciated each feature as though reading to children: eye movement tracking, background noise detection, an algorithm that scored every student for "focus integrity." In the sample dashboard, a grid of faces was sorted by risk level. Ashton paused the video and leaned closer. Seven of the nine faces in the red column had dark skin, exactly like the stock-photo class the company had chosen to illustrate it. He knew enough about how these systems learned to know that might mean nothing, and also that it might mean everything.

He called Hasan, who picked up mid-chew, half a sandwich audible in the background. "Are you seeing this Sentinel thing?" Ashton asked. "Look at the demo, minute two-forty. Tell me what you notice about who's flagged."

There was a silence long enough that Ashton checked whether the call had dropped. Then Hasan said, "They're all Black or brown. Every one." A pause. "Could be random. It's nine faces."

"Could be random," Ashton agreed. "Or it could be what happens when nobody checks. And they roll it out Monday."

Julian joined the call from his phone, lying on his bedroom floor, his face a pale oval against the ceiling. He'd already drafted a petition, all-caps, demanding the school "BAN SENTINEL NOW." Ashton read it and felt his enthusiasm curdle slightly. "It's not that simple," he said. "Half our class cheated last spring when everything was unproctored. The teachers know it. If we just say no, they'll hear yes to cheating."

"So we do nothing?" Julian's ceiling loomed as he sat up. "The whole thing is automated. Nobody even decides who gets flagged. A model decides, and a model can't be reasoned with."

Hasan, who had finished the sandwich, said what he always said in these arguments, which was the boring true thing: "It's new. Nobody knows what it'll actually do yet. Maybe the bias thing doesn't show up with real data. Maybe it's worse. You can't tell before it's running."

Ashton pulled up a search window while they argued, typing combinations of words like technology too late to change and rules before effects known. The fourth result was a scan of an old book, someone named David Collingridge, 1980. He skimmed the preview, then read the sentence twice, then a third time, because it seemed to have been written about exactly this week. "Guys," he said, and waited until Julian's ceiling stopped moving. "There's a thing called the Collingridge dilemma. It's from 1980. When a technology is new, its effects are hard to predict, but by the time the effects are clear, it's hard to change." He read it off the screen slowly, the way you'd read a verdict.

"That's it," Julian said. "That's literally it. So it's already too late."

"No." Ashton was surprised at how certain he sounded, because inside he wasn't. "It's too late for the tech that's already everywhere. Sentinel is Monday. We're at the beginning, not the end. It's too early to know what it does and it's the last moment it's still easy to change. That's the gap we're standing in." He heard himself and winced a little, and Hasan laughed at him, but nobody contradicted it.

They worked until almost eleven. Julian's petition became a letter, lowercase, addressed to the principal, with a paragraph Ashton wrote asking for three things: a public test of the flagging rates across student groups, an opt-in pilot instead of a mandate, and a human review of every flag before any consequence. Hasan found the company's contract with a nearby district, which had quietly dropped the microphone feature after complaints, and pasted the link. Progress felt glacial, one clause at a time, but it moved. Julian asked whether a letter counted as deterrence against bad tech or just a polite scream into a folder, and Hasan said probably both.

Ashton added a line at the end, after the three demands, admitting what the letter couldn't claim: that they did not yet know whether the system was biased, only that by the time they found out for certain, untangling it would be far harder than asking now. He attached the 1980 citation, then hovered over the send button, reread the principal's address, and checked it twice against the school website.

He pressed send. On the screen, in the folder called Drafts, nothing was left.

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: The relational model of databases was introduced by IBM researcher Edgar F. Codd in a 1970 paper, 'A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks'.
story:
Victoria had until midnight to submit the assignment, and her grandfather's dining table, with its lace cloth and its smell of pencil shavings and menthol, was the quietest place left. The prompt seemed almost like a trick: join two tables and return only the customers who had never ordered anything. She had the customers file open on her laptop, forty names in one rectangle, and the orders file in another, and no idea how to ask one question of both at once.

She had come out here partly for the silence and partly because her grandfather kept paper ledgers from the years he sold seed corn by mail, and she hoped that seeing the problem in his old columns might loosen it. He shuffled out with tea he called "the good kind, from before," and watched her scroll. "You're frowning at squares," he said. "In my day the squares were boxes, and inside them were index cards."

"That's kind of what I'm trying to figure out," she said. "Why squares at all. Why is everything tables? Who decided that?"

The question had been bothering her since Tuesday, when Lyndon had leaned across the lab and said the whole system felt arbitrary, like organizing a library by shoe size. Kellan had argued back that it obviously wasn't arbitrary, that somebody had engineered it, though he couldn't say who. Victoria had refused to pick a side, mostly because neither of them had any evidence, and the argument had gone on so long that Mr. Traoré, the neighbor who taught at the college and borrowed her grandfather's ladder more than anyone should, rapped on their shared fence and told them to settle it with sources.

Mr. Traoré was in the garden now, actually, on the riparian strip of shade along the back fence where the creek kept the soil dark. She carried her laptop out to him. "Do you know why databases are tables? Like who thought of it?"

He wiped his hands on his knees. "Codd," he said. "The relational model of databases was introduced by IBM researcher Edgar F. Codd in a 1970 paper, 'A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks.' The library will have it." Then he went back to his tomatoes, offering nothing further, which was his way of making her do the work.

So she did the work. The paper was dense, full of terms she had to transliterate slowly into her own notes, normal forms and relations laid out like proofs, and somewhere around page three she understood that the tables weren't boxes at all. They were statements. Every row was a small true sentence, customers are these people, orders are these events, and the joining was a way of letting the sentences speak to each other. It was less like filing and more like translation. She sat with that for a while, holding Lyndon's it's arbitrary next to Kellan's it's engineered, and found she could finally put them together: it was engineered, deliberately, by a person, which meant it could be criticized and rebuilt, and that made it both true things at once. Whether Codd's choice was the best choice, whether something else could have carried the same weight, stayed open, and she let it stay open.

Then the assignment turned concrete in her hands. She typed the join, customers on the left, orders on the right, keeping every customer whether or not an order matched, and filtering for the ones whose order columns came back empty. The engine returned three names. To test it, she pulled her grandfather's ledger down from the shelf and ran her finger down his customer column, then his order column, the whole machination of rubber bands and margin notes that had stood in for a database for thirty years. There, in his precise hand: a customer listed for years who had never once bought. Mrs. Adeyemi, two streets over, who took the catalog every spring and ordered nothing, and whom he still mailed by hand.

"Grandpa," she called toward the kitchen, "why do you keep sending these to her if she never orders?"

He came and looked at the ledger, then at her screen, at his own quiet absence of sales rendered as two empty columns. "Because she writes back," he said. "Not about seed. About her garden, her late husband. The catalog is just how the letters start."

Victoria submitted the query with ninety seconds to spare, and got the confirmation email almost instantly, timestamped before midnight by exactly one minute. She was still smiling at it when Lyndon texted: the professor had just posted that the due date was extended to Friday. She looked at the extension notice, then at her screen, at the join she had fought all evening to understand, and then at the three names, one of which was already a person she now wanted to meet.

"Set another place for tea," her grandfather said from the kitchen. "I'm walking the catalog over to Mrs. Adeyemi's while the light lasts. You can carry the good kind."

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: Steelmanning is the practice of restating an opposing argument in its strongest form, even stronger than the other person put it, before responding to it.
story:
Julia had prepared her rebuttal on the bus, in the margins of a photocopied article about highway tolls, and by the time the debate began she had underlined everything twice, which meant nothing was emphasized at all. The resolution was that cities should charge drivers for entering their downtown cores. She was on the side defending the drivers, which was unfortunate, since she didn't drive and privately thought tolls were a fine idea.

Maelys opened for the affirmative, all confidence and index cards. She cited congestion data from three cities, then made the mistake of dressing it up. "Congestion pricing," she said, "would transform the very texture of urban life." Julia wrote texture of urban life in her notes and drew a small coffin beside it.

When Julia stood for cross-examination, she abandoned her margin scribbles and asked, "Do you want me to answer your argument, or the version you'd make if you had another week and a better thesaurus?"

Maelys blinked. Mr. Ong, seated at the side table with a timer he never seemed to start on time, leaned forward.

"I don't understand the question," Maelys said.

"Your strongest point is the data. The part about texture is decoration. If I answer the decoration, I look clever and we both waste the round. So I'd rather answer the data." Julia paused, aware that her voice had gone flat, the way it did when she was about to be either right or insufferable. "Steelmanning," she said. "It's what Mr. Ong's handout called it, restating your argument in its strongest form, even stronger than you put it, before responding. I'm trying it."

Mr. Ong's handout, in fact, was two pages of squint-inducing photocopy that most of the class had recycled in September. Julia had read it in October, on the worst possible night, and she thought of it now.

Her father had stood in the kitchen holding her curfew proposal the way a customs officer holds a suspicious passport.
