Eleven thirty, she'd argued, was reasonable for a sixteen-year-old on weekends, and he'd said something about responsibility, something about trust being earned, and then something grandiose about the streets after dark that she'd laughed at out loud. The argument had ended in the usual place, which was nowhere. But sitting upstairs afterward, still angry, she'd found herself going over his half of it, trying to restate it so it would be worth defeating, because beating the version with the stuff about the streets after dark felt like fencing a scarecrow. Trust being earned, she'd written in her notebook. That was the real argument. Being somewhere reachable, at a predictable hour, was how you earned the next hour. She'd gone downstairs, said, "What you mean is, you can't extend trust you can't see," and watched his face do something complicated, halfway between defeat and relief. They'd settled on eleven fifteen. Nobody had claimed victory. It was the only argument she'd ever enjoyed.

In the gym, Maelys was waiting. "Fine," she said. "Steelman me."

Julia took a breath and laid it out. "The data says congestion drops when drivers pay to enter the core. Beyond that, the strongest version isn't even about traffic. It's that roads are a scarce resource, and prices are how we allocate scarce resources without rationing by patience or luck. The people who value the trip most are the ones who pay. That's your argument. That's better than texture."

Jaeden, seated on Julia's side of the aisle, muttered, "Traitor," with something like admiration.

She turned to him, since her time had begun. "And against it: a price sorts by value only if value and money are the same thing, which they aren't. A nurse driving in for a night shift values the trip more than a consultant driving in for lunch, and the toll doesn't care. So the question isn't whether pricing works, it's who it works on." She heard her own voice and stopped, briefly, worried it sounded rehearsed. It wasn't. She was building the bridge as she stood on it.

Maelys, to her credit, demurred from the easy comeback, the one about buses. " exemptions," she said instead. "You exempt the shift worker. The consultant pays."

"Then the consultant lobbies for the exemption," Julia said, "and you're arguing about the list forever."

"Then you argue about it with evidence," Maelys said, "not with an adage about how all lists grow corrupt."

"I didn't quote an adage."

"You were about to. It was in your posture."

The timer, which Mr. Ong had finally started, buzzed. Julia sat down beside Jaeden, who slid his notes toward her without comment. In them he had written, in the margin, She's better at your side than you are.

The rebuttal round came, and Julia answered the data point by point, conceded the part about scarce resources, and proposed the exemption list as a conditional: if the city could keep it clean, pricing might be fair, and if it couldn't, the toll was a tax on being needed. She didn't know which condition held. She said so, into the microphone, and watched Maelys smile for the first time all afternoon.

Mr. Ong stopped the timer and made a mark in his book. "For the record," he said, "I recycled most of those handouts in October and I don't know where that copy came from."

Julia looked at the photocopied article in her lap, at her own margins, full of underlines that now meant something. "I'll trade you," she said, holding it up. "Eleven fifteen, and it's yours."

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: If the forward reaction is exothermic, raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium toward the reactants, because the system absorbs the added heat by running in reverse.
story:
Robert set the two sealed tubes on his grandfather's kitchen table, next to the pill organizer and the single cup the old man allowed himself in the morning. The house was cold the way it always was, his grandfather keeping the thermostat at sixty like a man practicing some private ascetic discipline, and Robert had already decided this was an advantage. Cold was data. Cold was a variable he could use.

The tubes had come from the chemistry room, signed out under Ms. Rivera's name after he'd promised, in writing, not to open them. Each held the same reddish brown gas, the equilibrium mixture he'd built his whole science fair project around. His board, folded in the back seat of his mother's car, said it plainly: HEATING THE TUBES IN WARM WATER WILL SHIFT THE EQUILIBRIUM TOWARD MORE N2O4, AND THE GAS WILL LIGHTEN. He'd rehearsed the demo twice at school. He'd rehearsed it wrong.

That morning at the fair, in the gym with the folding tables and the bad lighting, the tubes had darkened. Both of them. He'd dunked them in the warm bath, watched for the brown to fade, and instead the color had deepened like a bruise, and Bronwyn, at the next table, had looked over and said, "Was it supposed to do that?" and he'd stood there holding a result that called his entire poster a lie. Ms. Rivera had stopped in front of his board, read his prediction, read his data, and said only, "Interesting," which was worse than anything.

Now his grandfather shuffled in and put water on without a word, and Robert propped his phone against the sugar bowl and called Niko. The screen showed Niko's ceiling, then his face. "Show me again," Niko said. Robert held the tubes up side by side, one from the cold kitchen windowsill, one he'd kept in his pocket, warm from his body all afternoon. The pocket tube was darker. The windowsill tube, sitting at sixty degrees for three hours, was paler, browner edging toward colorless at the top.

"So heat makes it darker," Niko said. "Cold makes it lighter."

"Here's what I can't get around." Robert turned his poster board toward the camera. "I wrote the equation forward as N2O4 going to NO2. If that forward reaction is exothermic, if it gives off heat going forward, then heating the system would shift it back toward the reactants. The N2O4. The colorless side. That's exactly what happened."

"You're telling me you predicted the wrong direction?"

"I'm telling you I got the heat wrong. I treated heat like something the reaction wanted more of." Robert pulled the pocket tube out and set it on the windowsill next to the cold one, side by side, and a nascent certainty was forming in him, still fragile, still argumentative with itself. "It's the opposite. Raising the temperature pushes it toward the reactants, because the system absorbs the added heat by running in reverse."

"So your demo was backwards, but your data was right."

"My data was the only thing that was right."

Niko was quiet for a second, and Robert could hear a girl's laugh somewhere behind him, the fair still going on without him. "Are you going to fix the board?"

"Ms. Rivera already saw it."

"Then she already knows. Ask her."

Robert took the phone down the hall and called, and Ms. Rivera picked up on the second ring, gym noise behind her. "Robert. Your tubes came back, I hope."

"They're at my grandfather's. I think I know what happened. If the forward reaction is exothermic, raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium toward the reactants."

"It does," she said. There was a pause with a scoreboard buzzer in it. "Your written prediction was the error, not your observation. Bring the tubes Monday."

"Can I redo the fair?"

"I'll ask about the regional," she said, and then she equivocated, something about committees and deadlines and not wanting to promise what she couldn't control, and he let her trail off because the answer didn't matter as much as he'd expected it to an hour ago.

When he came back to the kitchen, his grandfather was sitting at the table with his tea, looking at the two tubes. The pocket tube had been on the sill for maybe ten minutes and Robert could already see it, faint but undeniable, lightening from the top down. His grandfather tapped the paler one with one finger.

"This one's from the cold house," the old man said. "Sixty degrees, same as every winter since your grandmother." He looked up. "So being cheap is good for something."

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: Earth's surface gives off heat as infrared radiation; greenhouse gases absorb much of it and re-emit it in all directions, including back down, which warms the lower atmosphere.
story:
The trail climbed through pines for the first mile, and Luke kept his eyes on Jolie's backpack because she had the printed graph folded in the side pocket, and because watching her backpack was easier than admitting he did not know what he would say at the top. Ms. Hosseini had set the terms on Monday, in the empty lab after everyone else left: they were all hiking to Miller's Lookout on Saturday, and if Luke could explain the greenhouse effect and read the carbon dioxide graph to her satisfaction before they turned around at the summit, she would enter a real grade instead of the incomplete. If he could not, the incomplete would become final on Monday. She said it without any of the disappointment she was entitled to, which was somehow worse.

"I still don't get what you got wrong," Dion said, hopping a root. "You wrote three pages. I saw you writing three pages."

"That was the problem," Jolie said. "Three pages of everything bouncing off the sky."

"It doesn't bounce," Luke said. "That's the part I don't have yet."

They stopped at a switchback where the ground had been worn down to bare rock, sun-warmed even in October, and Dion put his palm flat against it and held it there. "This rock is giving off heat," he said. "I can feel it from here. So why doesn't it all just go up and out? Space is cold. Hot goes to cold. That's like the one rule of the universe."

Luke started to give the answer he'd given on the test, about the sun and layers, and heard it fall apart even as he assembled it. Jolie sat down on the rock and took out the graph, holding it so the light caught it. The line ran along the bottom of the page for a while, almost flat, and then it bent upward, slowly at first, and then it didn't stop. "A century," she said. "This is carbon dioxide, every year, measured straight through. Look at the shape of it. Look at the last fifty years especially."

"It goes up," Luke said. "It goes up faster."

"So what does that do," Dion said, "if more of it just floats around up there?"

Luke looked at his own hand, held it above the warm rock, and thought about what the rock was sending toward his skin. Not warm air. Something else, something the rock gave off on its own, all the time, day and night. "The surface gives off heat as infrared radiation," he said slowly, testing each word like a plank across a creek. "That's what I'm feeling right now. The ground does it everywhere, all the time. It's how the Earth cools off."

"Okay," Dion said. "So it radiates up. Then?"

Luke tried to picture the infrared leaving the rock and rising, and then the air above it, and the gases mixed through it. He got it wrong, he could feel himself getting it wrong, the way he had in the test, and he stopped. "Someone told me once that the gases trap it like a blanket. That's not right either, is it. A blanket just sits there."

Jolie shrugged, which was her way of adjudicating between his answer and his pride without giving him either. "I'm not telling you. She won't want the blanket."

The word came to him from a diagram he'd half-looked at and half-ignored, three nights ago, at two in the morning, while the incomplete sat on his laptop screen like a veneer over everything else in his week, thin and glossy and hiding the fact that he hadn't understood any of it. The diagram had shown arrows. "Absorb," he said. "The greenhouse gases absorb much of the infrared. They take it in. And then they re-emit it. In all directions." He turned in a slow circle on the rock, pointing up, sideways, down. "All directions. Some of it goes on up and out, but some of it comes back down."

"That part," Dion said. "Back down. That's the part that matters, isn't it. Heat that was leaving, coming back."

"Which warms the lower atmosphere," Luke said. "The air down here. Where we are." He looked at the graph again, at the line bending upward, and for the first time the two things he'd memorized separately, the mechanism and the measurement, were not separate. More carbon dioxide in the air, and more of the surface's own infrared coming back down instead of escaping, and the same air they were breathing on this switchback holding a little more of it than the air his grandparents had breathed. He did not say any of this out loud. He just stood there with his hand out over the rock, feeling the warmth rising off it and imagining some fraction of that warmth turning around partway up and coming home.

They reached the lookout at ten to three. Ms. Hosseini was already there, eating an apple, and she raised her eyebrows at Luke the way she did in lab, which meant proceed. He laid the graph on the flat stone beside her, traced the line with one finger, and began. He told it plainly this time, the surface radiating infrared, the gases absorbing much of it and re-emit it in all directions, including back down, the lower atmosphere warming, and the line on the page climbing through a hundred years and climbing faster now. He left out the blanket. He left out the three pages. When he finished, Dion was grinning at him over Ms. Hosseini's shoulder, and Jolie was looking at the valley below them with the expression of someone who has decided to let events speak.

Ms. Hosseini put down the apple core. "One more question," she said. "What are you still unsure of?"

Luke looked out over the trees, the subterranean hum of the highway somewhere beneath them, and thought about it honestly. "Why it took me a semester to ask what the ground was doing under my own hand," he said. She took out her phone and opened the gradebook.

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: A video cannot be reverse-searched directly by most image engines, so fact-checkers take screenshots of key frames and search those images instead.
story:
The phone repair shop smelled of solder and lemon wipes, and Liam had learned, in his first week behind the counter, that Mr. Nur kept the radio tuned to a station nobody else liked and that this was only one of his idiosyncrasies. Another was the jar of mismatched screws by the register, labeled, in careful capitals, NOT FOR SALE. Liam was supposed to be logging a shipment of screens. Instead his phone kept buzzing, because Devon had sent a video to the whole group chat at 8:14 that morning and everyone was passing it along like a lit match.

The clip showed a flood swallowing a parking garage, brown water folding over a concrete ramp, cars nudging each other like cattle. Someone had captioned it "downtown last night, get out now," and half the chat had already forwarded it to their parents. Devon had added a row of exclamation points. Liam had typed "holy" and then deleted it, because something about the light in the video bothered him, though he could not have said what. He had almost hit share when he noticed the palm trees at the edge of the frame. There were no palm trees downtown. There were no palm trees anywhere within six hours of their town.

"Customers first," Mr. Nur said without looking up from a disemboweled tablet. His voice was mild, but Liam had learned that mild was as far as it went with him; the last teenager who'd worked here had described him as truculent, and Liam had looked the word up that night and decided it was unfair. Mr. Nur was not looking for fights. He simply did not perform patience he did not feel.

"Sorry." Liam set his phone face down on a roll of bubble wrap. A woman came in with a phone whose screen had gone green, and he wrote up her ticket, and he warmed the adhesive strips for a battery swap, and all the while the flood video kept accumulating replies in his pocket. Arlo had written, "my mom's already moving the car to the roof of her office building." That was the part that turned it from a video into a problem. People were doing things because of it.

When the shop emptied out, Liam pulled the clip up again and held the phone toward the back room. "Mr. Nur. Can I ask you something not about phones?"

"You may ask."

"This video. Everyone's sharing it. I want to check if it's real before I send it anywhere, but I don't even know where you'd start. It's not a picture." He felt clumsy saying it, like admitting he couldn't read.

Mr. Nur wiped his hands on a cloth and took the phone. He watched the water, thumbed the progress bar back, watched again. "You cannot put a video into an image search," he said, sliding the phone back. "Most of the engines won't take it. But the frames, those are images. So what do people do who check these things for a living?"

Liam looked at the screen, at the water frozen mid-swallow where Mr. Nur had paused it. "Pause it," he said slowly, "and take a screenshot, and search that." He did it: volume down, pause, the power and home buttons together, the little thumbnail shrinking into the corner. A picture of a picture. He dragged it into the search bar of the image engine on the shop's ancient desktop, because his own phone was due for its own repair, and waited while the fan under the desk growled.

The results came back in a stack. A weather site from three years ago. A news agency's gallery. A stock footage page selling the clip, tagged with the name of a coastal city and an old date, the whole event predating Liam's driver's license. The palm trees were right there in the second result, in daylight, unmistakable. He sat back on the stool and heard himself exhale.

"Arlo," he said, and typed with both thumbs. "It's from three years ago, it's not here, tell your mom to come off the roof." Then to the whole chat, with the links, and then, after a moment, one more line: "I almost sent it before I checked. Didn't even know how until ten minutes ago." He hesitated over that last sentence, finger hovering, because it made him look slow, and then sent it anyway. Devon replied with a single sheepish emoji. Somebody else sent the daylight photo back with the word "palm trees" and nothing else.

"There is a second question," Mr. Nur said, returning to his tablet. "Why did everyone believe it this morning, and why did they believe you this afternoon? Same people, same screen. Think about what underpins each of those." He said it the way he said everything, flat, almost bored, as though he were remarking on the weather, and Liam understood he was being handed something and could pick it up or not.

Liam thought about it while he finished the battery swap, the old adhesive peeling away in gray ribbons. Devon had believed the video because the water looked like water, because fear travels faster than checking does. They'd believed him because he'd brought them a screenshot and a date and a stack of sources, which felt like better footing, though he noticed, as he sealed the new battery down, that he couldn't fully say why. A picture of a screen could be doctored too; a date could be wrong; the stack of links could all be wrong together. He was sure about the palm trees. He was sure the flood wasn't last night. Beyond that, some uncertainty stayed open like the back of the phone in his hands.

At closing, Mr. Nur lined the mismatched screws along a magnet strip, one by one, and glanced at the counter where Liam had left the desktop running, the search results still glowing. "Tomorrow," he said, "someone will send you another one."

"Probably before noon," Liam said, and pulled the shop door shut behind them, checking the lock twice.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: Minnesota's Department of Transportation says the zipper merge, using both lanes up to the merge point and then taking turns, can cut a backup's length by as much as 40 percent.
story:
The laundromat on Franklin Avenue had a long, empty curb out front, and Sara had decided this made it the best place in the neighborhood to learn to parallel park. She set two plastic laundry baskets on the asphalt, seven feet apart or maybe eight, and backed her mother's station wagon between them while Everett sat on the hood of his own car eating sunflower seeds and offering commentary nobody had asked for.

"You're a full basket away from the curb," he said. "A dog could sleep in that gap. Two dogs."

"It's not about the dogs." She straightened the wheel, checked her mirrors, and felt the small private satisfaction of the wagon sliding in clean on the third try. The night air smelled of detergent and warm lint drifting from the propped door, and a dryer hummed somewhere behind it like a highway heard from three blocks away. She cut the engine and sat with her hands still on the wheel.

She had failed the road test once already, in June, on the merge onto Interstate 94. The examiner had said nothing dramatic about it, only marked the clipboard, and Sara had spent most of the summer trying not to reify that failure into a fact about herself, a fixed property like eye color. It was just a skill she hadn't learned yet. That was the maxim she repeated, and some days it even worked.

Guneet came out of the laundromat carrying a paper bag of wet socks she'd rescued from a machine that ate quarters, and stood at the curb watching Sara pull forward and back between the baskets. "You know what you actually need?" Guneet said. "You need to hear about my drive here. Construction on 35, two lanes going down to one, everybody sliding over a mile early like it's a fire drill, and this one guy in a disaffected-looking van just cruising all the way up the empty lane to the front. Everybody hated him. I kind of admired him."

"Was he right, though?" Sara said. "Or just rude?"

Guneet pulled out her phone, thumbs moving, and turned the screen around. Sara read it in the dome light spilling from the laundromat's windows: Minnesota's Department of Transportation recommended the zipper merge, using both lanes up to the merge point and then taking turns, and said it could cut a backup's length by as much as 40 percent. She read it twice, because it contradicted something she'd absorbed from every adult who'd ever driven her anywhere, which was that merging early was polite and merging late made you a bad person.

"Forty percent," Everett said, spitting a shell into the bag of socks Guneet was now holding at arm's length. "That's like if this line of cars went to the corner instead of past the bank."

"Zipper merge," Guneet said, tapping the screen. "That's what they call it."

They stood there in the detergent-smelling dark while Sara turned it over. The early mergers weren't wrong to want to feel considerate; the guy in the van wasn't wrong either, if the state's own numbers said his way left less car for everyone behind him. Maybe politeness and efficiency pointed in the same direction here and everyone had just been taught to feel the opposite. Or maybe it only worked if everybody did it, and she would be the sole believer in the empty lane, sailing past a line of people who thought she was a jerk. She couldn't decide, and she noticed she didn't entirely mind not deciding.

"Saturday," she said, taking the keys out of the ignition. "Retest. And if there's construction, I'm using both lanes up to the merge point and taking turns, and if the examiner fails me for it, I'm telling him the Department of Transportation said so."

"He's going to love that," Everett said.

"Then he can take it up with forty percent." She popped the trunk, gathered the laundry baskets, and carried them toward the door, socks and all, one basket balanced on her hip like a traffic cone she had finally learned to steer around.

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: Denmark, Norway and Sweden have no statutory national minimum wage; pay floors are instead set through collective agreements between unions and employers.
story:
The debate packet lay untouched in Noemie's bag for four days, which she told herself was strategy. Rest, she'd said to Diego on Thursday, you don't want to burn out before you burn in. That wasn't a real saying and he'd looked at her like she knew it wasn't. Now it was Monday, fifth period, and Ms. Schneider was writing pairings on the board, and Noemie still hadn't read past the first page, which was mostly a photograph of a picket line from 1937.

"Noemie and Gregory," Ms. Schneider said. "Resolving the minimum wage." Diego got the opposition bench with a girl whose name Noemie kept forgetting on purpose, or told herself she did. She sat down beside Gregory and pulled the packet out as if she'd been carrying it open.

The proposition was simple enough that she could argue it without reading anything: raise the wage floor, workers earn more. Gregory had the counterfile, a thick folder of printouts he'd annotated in pencil, which annoyed her because she'd decided weeks ago that Gregory was the kind of person who annotated things in pencil to show he could. She might have been unfair about that. She was unfair about a lot of people, she'd noticed, and then had to metabolize the unfairness later, usually at night, when it kept her up.

First exchange went to her. She talked about her cousin, who worked at a bakery and calculated her hours on her phone every Sunday night, and whose schedule changed so often the calculation never matched her paycheck. Good, concrete, the judges nodded. Gregory came back with small businesses and prices and unemployment, all of which Noemie privately suspected he was reciting rather than understanding, though she couldn't have said what understanding would look like in his voice as opposed to reciting, so she filed the suspicion away unevidenced.

Then he flipped to a page and said, "No high-wage country lacks a minimum wage." He said it flat, like closing a door.

Noemie opened her mouth. She was about to say "obviously," which was what she said when she hadn't checked, when something in the packet caught the light. She turned the page she was on. It was the comparative table she'd skipped four times. She ran her finger down the columns and stopped at the row for Denmark. Norway. Sweden. Her finger stayed there longer than it should have, long enough that Gregory noticed.

"What," he said.

"Nothing." She read it again. She'd assumed every country with decent pay had a legal floor; it had seemed tautological to her, almost, that a high-wage country would have written its wage floor into law. The table said otherwise. She checked the source at the bottom, a labour economics anthology, then checked whether the anthology was on Ms. Schneider's approved list, which it was, which she admitted to herself was not the same as checking whether it was true, and which she then decided was enough.

"Denmark, Norway and Sweden," she said slowly. "No statutory national minimum wage."

"That's wrong," Gregory said, but he leaned over to look, and his pencil annotations ran out two rows above.

She stood to give her rebuttal and found she didn't have one lined up. The judges waited. Ms. Schneider waited, arms crossed, doing the thing she did where she taught by withholding. So Noemie said it plainly, since the alternative was bluffing. "The proposition assumed a legal wage floor is the only floor. But in Denmark, Norway and Sweden, the pay floors get set another way, through collective agreements between the unions and the employers." She heard herself say it and wondered whether she was defending her side or abandoning it, whether raising the minimum wage was the point or whether the point was whatever arrangement got people paid, and she recognized, with a small cold drop, that she had never actually separated those two questions before, that she'd been arguing a slogan.

Diego, from the opposition bench, raised his hand even though it wasn't his turn, which was against every rule and completely like him. "So if we don't have that," he said, "if we don't have those agreements everywhere, then the law is doing the job the unions do there?"

"Or the law's a weaker version of it," Noemie said. "Or a different tool entirely. I don't know which." That last part came out before she could dress it up, and she watched it land on the room, on the judges, on Gregory, who had stopped annotating and was looking at her like she'd forfeited. Maybe she had. Her cousin's bakery wasn't in Denmark. The whole physiology of the debate, its heartbeat of winning, was telling her to pivot back to the safe ground of the paycheck story, the Sunday-night math, and she knew she could land it, she'd landed harder things.

The judges conferred in whispers. Ms. Schneider uncrossed her arms and wrote something on her clipboard, and Noemie, who had a practiced habit of reading Ms. Schneider's face and finding disapproval in it, found disapproval there and then wondered, for the first time all year, whether she was reading the face or reading herself into it.

"Final rebuttal, proposition," the head judge said.

Noemie looked down at the table again, the empty column where a number should have been for three countries, and the filled columns everywhere else.

"My cousin gets her schedule on Saturday night for the week that starts Sunday," she said. "And I keep thinking a law would fix that, and now I'm not sure a law fixes that. Now I think maybe what fixes it is people like her deciding together, except I don't know how you get from here to there, and I don't want to pretend I do."

Gregory shut his folder. "That's not a rebuttal."

"No," she said. "It's the first thing I've said all afternoon that I actually checked."

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: The US fairness doctrine, introduced in 1949, required broadcasters to air contrasting views on controversial public issues; the Federal Communications Commission abolished it in 1987.
story:
Elijah had the good table, the one by the window with two outlets, and he was not giving it up. He spread out his notes for the media unit essay while Pyper dropped her bag across from him with the sound of someone who intended to stay.

"You have to pick a topic," she said. "Ms. Bianchi said the draft's due Thursday."

"I have a topic." He turned his laptop so she could see the half-formed sentence on the screen. "Whether news coverage can be biased even when nobody at the paper is lying."

"That's not a topic, that's a coma." She slid the laptop back. "Also, Breanna's coming, and she's in a mood, so be nice."

Breanna arrived holding her phone like evidence at a trial. She sat down, pulled a granola bar apart, and put half in front of Elijah without being asked, which he took as a good sign. "Okay, so my uncle posted this thing about how the station in his city never covers the water cleanup, and my mom said it's because the station's owned by the same company that's being sued over the cleanup. And I said that can't be legal, and she said, watch, nobody checks." She looked up. "Can they just do that?"

"That's my topic," Elijah said.

"You can't own a topic."

He was already searching, half listening to Pyper tell Breanna about the granola bar situation in the vending machine, which had eaten her dollar. The library databases came up, and beside them the open web, where the same story about the water cleanup appeared on three different sites with three very different emphases. One called the lawsuit "frivolous." One called the contamination "alleged." He started a two-column note, because two columns was how his grandfather had taught him to think, and because his grandfather was the person to call anyway.

His grandfather answered on the second ring, too loud, as always, a raconteur who treated every phone call as a small performance. Elijah held the phone away from his ear and then back. "I'm at the library," he said quietly, and got shushed from the next table, which his grandfather found hilarious.

"Ask your question then, I'll whisper." He did not whisper. "News and who owns it. Right, well. When I was young, the TV stations had to give both sides. There was a rule called the fairness doctrine, nineteen forty-nine. Stations had to air contrasting views on controversial public issues. It was the Federal Communications Commission that made them do it." A pause, the sound of a chair creaking. "And the same commission abolished it, in nineteen eighty-seven. After that, nobody had to."

Elijah wrote it down fast, numbers first. "So what happened after?"

"That's your essay, not mine," his grandfather said, sounding pleased. "Come by Sunday. Bring the tall one."

He hung up and stared at his notes. Pyper leaned over. "Nineteen forty-nine to nineteen eighty-seven. That's most of a lifetime of both sides being required, and then it just stopped." She said it flatly, but her pencil was already moving; she copied the dates onto her own page without asking, which was Pyper's way of saying the topic was now real.

Elijah went back to the databases. The fairness doctrine was easy to find, easier than he expected, and the part that surprised him was not the rule itself but the argument around it, which was trenchant on both sides and circumscribed by nothing; people who wanted it gone said it chilled speech, people who wanted it kept said it was the only floor under public discourse, and both sides wrote as if the other were naive. He read two more articles while Breanna, calmer now, scrolled her uncle's station's ownership page and said, half to herself, "So it's not even a secret. It's all public, and it still doesn't change anything."

"Or it changes it slowly," Pyper said. "Or it would change it if people looked, and they don't."

"That's not the same as a conspiracy," Elijah said. "That's the opposite of a conspiracy. It's right there and nobody's hiding it."

Ms. Bianchi came by on her rounds, collected a stray coffee cup from their table with a look that spared them the lecture, and paused at Breanna's screen. "Ownership research," she said. "Good. Cite the filings, not the blogs." She moved on, and Breanna sat up straighter, because Ms. Bianchi's approval was rare enough to be currency.

Elijah drafted a paragraph. He wrote that the fairness doctrine had required contrasting views from 1949 until the Federal Communications Commission abolished it in 1987, and that ownership was now the lens his essay would test: whether a parent company's interests could shape a station's choices without anyone lying, and whether anything had replaced the old rule or only the market had. Then he stopped, because the honest sentence was harder. He did not know, yet, whether the ownership connection in Breanna's uncle's city was influence or coincidence, and he wrote that too, in smaller letters, at the bottom of the page: unresolved, for now.

"It's almost nine," Pyper said, stacking her books. "You're coming back tomorrow?"

"Sunday I'm at my grandfather's," Elijah said. "He wants to talk about it more."

"Tell him Breanna says thanks," Breanna said, zipping her bag. "Even though he shouts."

Elijah packed slowly, leaving the two-column notes on top so he'd see them first thing in the morning. At the door he looked back at the table by the window, still lit, and Pyper waved him on.

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: Code-switching is moving between two languages within one conversation; it is common among fluent bilinguals and is not by itself a sign of weak skill.
story:
Amelia had taped the debate prompt to her bathroom mirror three weeks ago: whether cities should ban single-use plastics. She could argue it in English until her voice gave out. Now she stood behind a folding table at the heritage festival with a paper sign reading "Debate en español" propped against a jar of pens, and her Spanish felt like a muscle beginning to atrophy from disuse, thinner every year since her grandmother stopped calling on Sundays.

"You're up in twenty minutes," Leticia said, dragging a second chair over. "Mr. Vargas already set the timer. Five minutes, entirely in Spanish, and he'll dock points for every English word."

"He said dock points?" Amelia asked, and Leticia nodded, grim. Behind them, the festival spread across the park: food stalls, a stage where a folk dancer's skirts caught the wind, a table of younger kids folding paper flowers. Mr. Vargas was judging the debate segment for the third year, and he had a reputation for stopping the clock and asking, pleasantly, whether a contestant wanted to try that sentence again.

Amelia ran her opening in her head. "Los plásticos de un solo uso dañan..." and then the word she wanted, the one that meant the slow accumulation of waste in rivers, kept sliding away from her. She had it in English, of course, had it with footnotes. In Spanish she had her grandmother's kitchen vocabulary, soft and specific, and nothing for policy at all.

"Anabelle's doing the opposing side," Leticia said. "She's nervous too. She told me she's been dreaming in Spanglish."

Anabelle arrived holding two paper cups of horchata, one of which she pushed into Amelia's hands. "I keep starting sentences one way and ending them the other," she admitted. "My mom says her whole office talks like that, but Mr. Vargas wants it pure."

"Pure," Amelia repeated. The word sat wrong with her, like a door that didn't quite close.

When her turn came, she stood at the front of the tent, faced the small folding chairs, and began. The first minute held. She laid out the problem of plastic in the ocean, her gestures doing half the work. Then Anabelle challenged her on the cost to small vendors, street sellers who couldn't afford the alternatives, and Amelia reached for the phrase that would concede the point while pivoting to subsidies, and nothing came. The tent was hot. A toddler dropped a cup somewhere behind her. "The vendors need..." she heard herself say, and the English words were out before she could stop them, "a gradual timeline, porque..." She caught herself, horrified, and Anabelle jumped on it instantly.

"That doesn't count," Anabelle said, not unkindly, turning to Mr. Vargas. "She broke the rule."

But a woman in the third row, older, with a lanyard from the community college, raised her hand. "Could I say something? I teach linguistics there." Mr. Vargas gestured for her to go ahead, though his timer stayed running. "What she just did has a name. It's called code-switching, moving between two languages within one conversation. It's common among fluent bilinguals, and it's not by itself a sign of weak skill." She said it simply, the way you'd hand someone a fact they'd dropped.

Anabelle looked at Amelia, and Amelia looked at Mr. Vargas, whose pen had stopped moving. "The rule stands for the competition," he said. "But the rule and the fact are two different things." He clicked the timer back on. "You have three minutes, Amelia. Continue."

She stood there a moment longer, and instead of retreating she took the risk the woman had handed her. "Lo que hice," she said slowly, "fue code-switching, y no significa que mi español sea débil." Her accent was not the issue and never had been; the issue was that she had been treating her two languages as rivals when they had always, in her grandmother's kitchen and in the community college hallway and probably in Anabelle's mother's office, been one continuous way of thinking. She argued the rest of the time in Spanish, and when a word failed her she circled it in Spanish rather than borrowing, slower but hers, and the vendors got their timeline.

Afterward, outside the tent, a boy from the audience told Anabelle her rebuttal had been petulant, and Anabelle told him, with great dignity, that he was an aesthete who cared more about how arguments sounded than whether they were true, and he had to look the word up on his phone.

Mr. Vargas posted the scores on the tent pole. Amelia's name was second. She didn't know yet whether she agreed with the rule, whether five pure minutes proved anything, or whether the mixing was its own kind of fluency that no contest had learned to measure. She lifted her cup of horchata toward Anabelle.

"Nosotras dos, otra vez el año que viene," she said.

"Deal," Anabelle said, and tapped her paper cup against it.

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: The US Federal Reserve began raising its policy rate from near zero in March 2022 and reached a range of 5.25 to 5.50 percent in July 2023.
story:
Vanessa's mother slid the two mortgage offers across the kitchen table the way she slid over bills she didn't want to read aloud, and Vanessa understood that the visit to the bank on Saturday was not optional. The numbers on the pages were not close. Her mother wanted to know which one was a trap, and she'd said, "You're the one taking economics," as though the class were a form of insurance. Vanessa had said she'd figure it out, and then spent Tuesday evening not figuring it out, because she could not answer the question underneath her mother's question: why the rates were so different from a few years earlier, and what had changed. She knew the words. She could say "monetary policy" in a sentence. She could not make the sentence do any work.

Mr. Kim had assigned the seminar weeks ago, and Vanessa had let it sit at the bottom of her backpack like a debt. Each student had to take one mechanism from the course and explain it to the room without notes. Hers was the transmission from a central bank's policy rate to inflation itself. When Alana heard the topic, she'd laughed and said, "Good luck, that's the one everyone pretends to understand," and Vanessa had laughed too, and then hadn't slept well.

On Wednesday she went to the library during lunch and found a chart she had skipped before. The Federal Reserve had begun raising its policy rate from near zero in March 2022, and by July 2023 it had reached a range of 5.25 to 5.50 percent. She copied the numbers onto her palm with a pen because her notebook was in her locker, and she sat looking at them, at the steepness implied between the two dates, feeling something assemble itself slowly and then all at once. It was not that she hadn't known. It was that the numbers made the knowing hers.

From across the library, Alana watched Vanessa stare at her own hand for two full minutes, and she understood, without saying so, that something had shifted. Alana had her own topic, reserve requirements, and her own quiet problem: her father had been talking at dinner about refinancing, and his voice had that false-cheerful tone he used when the numbers were against him. She wondered whether Vanessa knew that her mother had picked up extra shifts at the clinic. Alana knew because her own mother worked there. She picked up her bag, crossed the room, and sat down without asking.

"You look like you found something," Alana said.

Vanessa turned her palm over. "The Fed started from basically nothing in March 2022. Near zero. Two years from that to five and a half percent. That's the whole cliff my mom's mortgage offers are standing on." She said it fast, testing it aloud, and Alana heard the other thing underneath it, the thing Vanessa hadn't said, which was that she was scared of Saturday, and that understanding the mechanism would not lower a single rate by a single point.

"Explain the middle part, then," Alana said. "The part between the cliff and prices."

That was the crux, and Vanessa knew it was the crux. She started twice, abandoned a bromide about supply and demand that Mr. Kim had written on the board and crossed out himself, and finally said, "It works through us. Through what people decide not to buy." Even as she said it she winced, because the sentence was true and incomplete at once. She believed it the way she believed her own handwriting: recognizably hers, possibly wrong at the edges. There were pieces she could not yet connect, rooms of the argument she could describe only by their doorways, and she decided she would say so out loud in the seminar rather than paper over it. Alana nodded slowly, the way she nodded at true things that didn't help.

At Thursday's presentation, Vanessa stood up with nothing in her hands. She laid out the hike from near zero to 5.25 to 5.50 percent, and then she built the chain step by step, costlier borrowing, slower spending, cooler demand, and when she reached the link she couldn't complete, she said, "Here's where I'm honest, or here's where I fake it, and I'd rather be honest." Alvin, in the second row, exhaled the way people do when they've been bracing for a bluff. Mr. Kim said nothing, which everyone in the room knew was the highest grade he gave in the moment.

On Saturday, at the bank, the loan officer slid a new page across the desk and began to expostulate about prepayment penalties, about the market, about how nobody could have predicted any of it. Vanessa let him finish. Then she looked at the rate on the page, and at her mother's hands folded around the pen, the knuckles gone pale the way they did, and she understood, finally, the fact she had been withholding from herself all week: this wasn't a seminar question. The hours at the clinic had been cut in October. The house was on the table.

"Take your time," her mother said quietly, watching her face. "Read it to me."

Vanessa pulled the page closer and began with the rate.

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: A NOT IN subquery returns no rows at all if the subquery's list contains even one NULL, a common trap when searching for missing matches.
story:
Mackenzie got the job at the phone repair shop in June, three afternoons a week behind the counter, logging cracked screens and water-damaged batteries into a database Ms. Russo had built years ago and never cleaned. By August Ms. Russo had given her the passwords and a problem: a mailing list for everyone who had signed up but never brought a device in. "The loyal ones get a card," she said. "The ones we've never seen get a coupon. Two tables, one list. You said you're taking computer science in the fall."

She worked on it in the back room, at the desk between the shelves of diaphanous screen protectors still in their plastic sleeves, with a SQL book Kaydence had lent her, its spine cracked at the chapter on subqueries. Kaydence came by on Thursday with two iced coffees and sat on the stool beside her. "You want a left join," Kaydence said. "Customers on the left, orders wherever they land, and you keep the ones where nothing lands."

Mackenzie tried it. The join worked, more or less, but the chapter had spent two pages on another method, the one where you write WHERE customer_id NOT IN and then, in parentheses, the whole list of customers from the orders table. It looked cleaner to her. It read like English: customers who are not in the orders. She typed it, ran it, and the grid below the query came up completely empty. Not one row. Not even the coupon customers she knew existed, like the man who had signed up in July and then gone to a different shop.

"Delete the query," Kaydence said. "It's haunted."

"It's not haunted, it's wrong somewhere." Mackenzie scrolled the orders table by hand, row by row, forty at a time. Somewhere in the middle of August there was an order with no customer typed in at all, the customer field just blank, the way it looked when a phone was dropped off in a rush and the name never got entered. She kept scrolling and found a second one, and then a third, all from the week Ms. Russo had been at her sister's wedding and a temp had run the counter.

She looked at the blank fields for a while. Then she typed a smaller query, one that pulled only the customer values from the orders table, and ran it. The list came back with numbers and, in the middle of them, three empty cells. She sat back with her coffee melting on the desk and thought about her politics teacher from senior year, who had spent a unit arguing that a blank ballot and a no vote were different things, that a theocracy and an elected government could both arrive at the same law by incompatible logics. She had written a paper about it and gotten a B plus and the comment that she was more interested in the disagreement than in deciding anything. That had stung at the time. Sitting here now, it seemed like the only honest way to think.

She changed one word. WHERE customer_id NOT IN became a different construction, the join Kaydence had suggested, customers on the left, orders on the right, keeping the rows where no order attached itself. She ran it. The grid filled: eleven customers, including the man from July, including a woman named in the system only as Alexanne R., who had signed up at a street fair booth in the spring and never come in. Mackenzie checked the list against the orders table twice, and the blanks were still there, three of them, and the list still came back whole.

Kaydence leaned over her shoulder. "So what was it? The parentheses?"

"The blanks," Mackenzie said. "If the list has even one NULL in it, the whole query returns nothing at all."

"That's deranged."

"It's a rule. It's in the book, probably, in a footnote I skipped." She found the footnote, one sentence near the bottom of a page, confirming what she had watched happen. She read it twice and closed the book. It was strange to her that she had needed the afternoon to learn one sentence, and stranger that the afternoon had been worth it, that she trusted the rule now in a way she would not have if the footnote had come first. She could not have said which method was better in general. The join had worked here. She suspected that somewhere else, on some other pair of tables, it would be the slower one, and she would have to decide again.

Ms. Russo came through the back room with an armful of bubble wrap and read the list upside down. "Eleven. Alexanne, I remember her, she wanted her screen fixed by the fair and I couldn't do it." She copied the names onto a pad. "Print this for me, and put the blanks on my desk, the three orders with no customer. Those are real people too, whoever they are."

Mackenzie printed the list and queued the blank orders for the desk. Kaydence held the door with her hip, coffee cups stacked, and called from the doorway that she was leaving before the register did something else haunted. Mackenzie stayed another twenty minutes with the query open on the screen, the two tables and the join, and saved it under a file name she almost laughed at, then didn't, then typed anyway: lesson_one.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm, outside the mitochondria, and splits one glucose molecule into two pyruvate molecules for a net gain of two ATP.
story:
Victoria had walked the Miller's Creek trail every Sunday since she was ten, but she had never brought her chemistry folder along before. She spread it on the flat stone by the second footbridge, the one the dog walkers called the lecture hall because teenagers from the high school claimed it every spring to cram for finals. Mylie sat cross-legged on the moss with a sandwich, and Declan stood at the railing, skipping stones into the creek with the particular violence of someone who had failed a biology quiz.

"Draw it again," Mylie said through peanut butter. "The whole cell. You said it helps to see it."

Victoria uncapped a marker. The cell took shape under her hand: the wobbly membrane, the blob of nucleus, the kidney-bean mitochondria with their folded insides. Somewhere in that drawing, she knew, was the answer to the question she had gotten wrong, and the tutoring job that came with it. Ms. Yilmaz had offered her twenty dollars a session to help a freshman who was drowning in biology, and Victoria, currently so impecunious she was saving lunch money for a bus pass to the college tour in April, had said yes before remembering that saying yes meant knowing the material herself.

"So where does the first step go?" Mylie asked, leaning over the stone. "The breaking down of glucose. You put an arrow last time."

Victoria's marker hovered. In her mind she could see the graded quiz, red ink circling her diagram, the arrow she had drawn straight into the mitochondria as if glucose walked in the front door and came out as energy. She had been so certain. She had even labeled it.

"I put it inside," she said. "Mitochondria. Because that's the powerhouse, right? That's what everyone says."

Declan stopped skipping stones. "That's what I put too. I got it wrong."

"And the freshman I'm tutoring tomorrow," Victoria said, "is going to put it inside too. I'd bet anything. It's the obvious place." She stared at the drawing, at the pale space between the cell membrane and the organelles, that nothing-area she had always thought of as filler. The cytoplasm. She said the word out loud, slowly, testing it.

Mylie had gone quiet in the way she did when she was actually thinking, which was different from her quiet when she was bored, and Victoria had learned to tell them apart over four years of friendship. Mylie picked up the second marker, the blue one, and drew a small line in that filler space. "My sister made me a study sheet," she said. "I memorized it for her. Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm, outside the mitochondria, and it splits one glucose into two pyruvate molecules, for a net gain of two ATP. I don't know what most of that means. I just know the words."

Victoria wrote it underneath in her smallest print. Net gain of two. Two pyruvate. Outside the mitochondria. It was strange, she thought, the way the fact sat there, plain as a stone, neither impressed by the mitochondria nor ashamed of the cytoplasm. It simply happened where it happened, and her certainty had been a kind of story she'd told herself, a drawing with verisimilitude but no truth. She thought of her father, who loved to contextualize everything, war and weather and his own bad knees, placing each thing in its history so it made sense; maybe facts needed that too, needed to be placed, not just remembered.

"Okay," she said, and redrew the arrow. First step in the cytoplasm, glucose splitting, two pyruvate. Then the pyruvate moving inward, toward the mitochondria, toward whatever came next, which she still couldn't quite see. "I know where it starts now. I don't know the whole road yet."

"Twenty dollars to know the whole road," Declan said, and for the first time all afternoon he laughed.

"Ten," Victoria said. "I'm splitting it with Mylie. She's the one with the sister."

The light was going amber over the creek, and Mylie started folding the sandwich wrapper, and Victoria looked at the drawing a moment longer, the blue line in the blank space, the arrow pointing in. Tomorrow she would tell the freshman to start in the cytoplasm, and after that she would learn the rest, step by step, the same way anyone learns anything. She capped the marker and said, "Same time next Sunday? Bring the study sheet."

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: Integrating a velocity function over a time interval gives the displacement, which is the area under the velocity-time graph.
story:
The math club met on Tuesdays in room 214, where the desks had been pushed into a horseshoe and the radiator clanked like it was trying to contribute. Alexis arrived early, before Ms. Boateng had even unlocked the cabinet of graphing calculators, because she had something folded in the front pocket of her backpack and she wanted a good seat when she unfolded it.

The paper was a crumpled notebook page. On Sunday she had driven with her grandmother to the audiologist in Harlow, two hours each way, and her grandmother had announced halfway there that the car's odometer was "not to be trusted since the incident," whatever the incident was. So Alexis had done the only thing that seemed reasonable at the time: she had watched the speedometer and written down the speed every minute. Sixty numbers in each direction, in her grandmother's looping shorthand dictation, because her grandmother insisted on calling them out like bingo.

"That's deranged," Byron said when she smoothed the page flat on a desk. "I mean that as a compliment." He leaned over her shoulder, radiating the sardonic certainty of someone who had already finished the calculus unit and wanted everyone to know it. "Sixty data points. You could have just read the mile markers."

"Which are also not to be trusted since the incident," Alexis said. "She's very clear on that."

Kabir pulled a chair up beside her, spinning a pencil. Kabir's actual agenda for the afternoon was the regional problem set, due Friday, on which he was currently three points behind a girl from Pemberton and visibly suffering for it. But he looked at her page for a long moment and then stopped spinning the pencil. "Wait. Speed every minute. That's a graph."

"That's a graph," Alexis agreed.

Ms. Boateng circulated with her mug of tea, pausing at each cluster long enough to see whether anyone was stuck but not long enough to hover. When she reached their desk, Alexis had already drawn axes in her own notebook: time along the bottom, minute by minute out to sixty, speed up the side. She had plotted a scatter that wobbled up around the stretch of highway and sank to nearly zero in the town at each end.

"Connect them," Kabir said. "It's basically a curve."

"It's a hideous curve," Byron said. "It looks like a mountain range designed by committee."

Alexis connected the points anyway. Then she sat back and looked at the shape, the ragged hill of it, and felt the actual question arrive in her head with a weight she hadn't expected. She knew how to find the slope of a curve at a point. She had drilled that for weeks. But slope was about how fast things changed, and what she wanted here was something else. She wanted the total. She wanted to know how far the car had actually traveled, and she had a feeling, half-formed and slightly embarrassing, that the answer was somehow the region under the line rather than any single point on it.

"So here's the thing," she said slowly. "In physics we did position and velocity. And the area under a velocity-time graph is the displacement." She said the word displacement carefully, the way you handle something you believe but haven't yet tested. "So if my graph is right, the area under it should be how far we actually went."

Byron opened his mouth, and Alexis held up a hand. "Don't explain it to me. I want to get it wrong first."

He closed his mouth, which for Byron was an act of significant restraint, and Kabir grinned at him as if to say, now you know how it feels.

Ms. Boateng said nothing at all. She set her mug down on the corner of the desk, an act Alexis understood as permission, and went to help a boy at the far end who was trying to prove a lemma about triangle inequality and proving it badly.

Alexis worked in rectangles. If the car was going fifty-five for a whole minute, that minute was a thin column, fifty-five wide by one minute tall. She added up the columns. Then she did it again, taking the speed at the end of each minute instead of the beginning, and got a slightly different number, and then a third time using the average of the two, and the numbers leaned toward each other like they were converging on something. Byron, unable to bear it, took over the arithmetic for the middle stretch while Kabir did the last fifteen, muttering about Pemberton the whole time, and Alexis noticed that he had abandoned his problem set entirely, which meant his three-point deficit was getting worse while he sat there, and that he didn't seem to mind.

"How far do you think it actually was?" Kabir asked.

"My grandmother says forty-one miles. She says it the way other people say their wedding date."

The final sum came out to a hair under forty-one miles, and Alexis checked it twice, and then she just looked at it. The fact that the odometer was broken and the mile markers were suspect and her grandmother's memory was confident but elderly, and yet the area under a wobbly hand-drawn curve had landed within spitting distance of all of them, made something shift in how she thought about what a graph was for. She was still uncertain about the honest part, the part where the rectangles were only an approximation, where the true answer lived in a limit she couldn't yet compute. She said so out loud.

"It's not exact," she said. "I don't love that."

"It's exact enough to catch a liar," Byron said. "Ask the odometer how it feels."

Ms. Boateng drifted back, glanced at the notebook, at the three of them still crowded around it, at Kabir's untouched problem set, and raised her mug slightly, as if toasting them or perhaps the radiator. Then Alexis took out her phone and photographed the page, and texted the picture to her grandmother with a single line: I can prove the incident was 41 miles.

Her grandmother replied within a minute, in all caps, EXCORIATE THE MECHANIC FOR ME, and Alexis laughed so suddenly that Byron jumped, and she turned the phone around so they could all see it, still laughing, while Kabir quietly pulled his problem set back in front of him and began, finally, to write.

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: Of the common disturbances to an equilibrium, a change in temperature is the only one that changes the value of the equilibrium constant K.
story:
The kettle had not yet boiled when Emile spread his notes across his grandfather's kitchen table, beside the bowl of walnuts the old man cracked every afternoon with a small brass hammer. The house smelled of woodsmoke and the lavender his grandmother had dried in bundles from the porch rail two summers before she died, and the silence of it was the reason Emile came here to study instead of staying at home, where his younger brothers extruded noise the way a press extrudes hot metal, continuously and without apparent effort. He had the exam on Monday. Kade was coming over with the practice problems.

Kade arrived with his bike helmet still clipped to his backpack and a paper bag of the lemon candies they had eaten all through AP Chemistry, and they settled into the rhythm of the work, trading equations, arguing about sig figs. The fourth question gave them an equilibrium, the same one they had solved in class on Tuesday, and then said the mixture was heated. Emile wrote the old value of K at the top of his page and carried it through every line, adjusting concentrations in the direction heat would push them, arriving at answers with a certain satisfaction, the satisfaction of method.

"Half of mine are different," Kade said, chewing his candy. He turned his sheet sideways, as though the disagreement might resolve itself viewed from another angle. "Same directions as you for the shifts. Different numbers everywhere."

Emile's grandfather passed through the kitchen for more walnuts, said nothing, and settled into his chair by the window with a crossword, his saturnine face giving away nothing about whether he was listening. He had taught chemistry for thirty-one years in a school two towns over, and Emile had grown up with a superstition about doing homework in his line of sight, a feeling that wrong answers might be visible to him the way weather is visible to farmers.

Emile checked the shifts first, because that was the argument he trusted himself to win. Heating an endothermic reaction drove it forward; both of them had that. The concentrations followed. But the numbers, he saw now, were built on K, and K had come straight from Tuesday, from the room-temperature problem, unexamined. He sat back. "I kept the same K."

"So?"

"So maybe that's the thing." He said it slowly, testing it the way you test ice. "Concentration changes, pressure changes, those don't touch K. The system just moves. But temperature is different. Temperature changes the value of the equilibrium constant itself. That's why my numbers are all wrong and the directions are all right." Kade looked at him, then at his own sheet, then began crossing things out with the particular violence of a person converting error into certainty. Emile did not feel certain, though. He felt the shape of something true under his hands, and he wanted to check it against something outside himself.

From the window chair, the old man watched the two heads bent over the table and remembered a January afternoon forty years gone, a borrowed lab in an unheated wing of a college, where a younger version of himself had run the same reaction at three temperatures and stared at the three different constants in his notebook as though one of them must be a mistake. He had wanted it not to be true, that a single number he had trusted could depend on something so ordinary as warmth. It had been, in a small way, the end of a belief that the world kept its agreements unconditionally. He turned a page of his puzzle and decided he would say nothing unless asked, because a fact a man hands you is lighter than a fact he lifts himself, and Emile, hunched and scowling at the paper, was lifting it.

Emile found his phone and scrolled to the message thread with Ms. Navarro, the one where she had answered his question about the exam format at eleven at night with a single colloquialism he would not repeat to his mother, and he typed out the question and set the phone face-up between them. They worked the problem again with a new variable in place of the old constant, and Emile felt the two ways of thinking settle next to each other without quite merging, the rule about shifts in one hand and the fact about K in the other, neither overriding the other, each one useful at its own moment. The phone buzzed. A single word glowed on the screen, and Kade leaned over to read it, and Emile read it aloud anyway. "Yes."

activity: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
knowledge_domain: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
fact: One Vindolanda tablet is a birthday party invitation from Claudia Severa to Sulpicia Lepidina, written around 100 CE, with closing lines that are among the earliest known Latin writing by a woman.
story:
The argument started over a photocopy. Mr. Takahashi had laid out six documents on the long table at the back of the history classroom, reproductions of things Faith was supposed to interrogate like a suspicious witness: a charcoal rubbing, a ship's manifest, two maps that disagreed about the same coastline, a monk's chronicle, and a photograph of a thin wooden scrap no bigger than a bookmark. Faith took the maps first, because maps felt like facts, and facts felt like ammunition.

"They can't both be right," she said, turning them toward Veronica. "The river's on the east side in one and the west in the other."

"Maybe the river moved," Veronica said.

"Then which map is the truth?"

Mr. Takahashi passed behind them without stopping. He had a way of doing that, orbiting the room, letting the silence do the teaching. Faith found it theatrical. She wanted him to just tell them which map was right, the way a coach calls a foul, so the game could continue.

The problem was the essay due Friday. Faith had claimed a thesis with real appetite: that history was a science, and that where historians disagreed, one of them was simply sloppy. She had written four paragraphs of it the night before, and the paragraphs had gone well, which was exactly the trouble. They were good paragraphs. She did not want them to be wrong. Across the room, Alayna was hunched over her own draft, pencil moving in short strokes, and Faith remembered that Alayna's thesis was the mirror of hers: that the past was unknowable, that every account was invention, that nothing survived. Faith thought that was lazy. Alayna probably thought Faith was arrogant. Neither of them had said so out loud, which made it worse.

Faith picked up the wooden scrap last, out of tidiness more than interest. The caption said it was one of the Vindolanda tablets, thin leaves of wood found where Roman soldiers had dropped their letters in the mud. She read the translation twice, and the second time she stopped reading like a student and started reading like a eavesdropper.

"Listen to this," she said, and both Veronica and Alayna looked up, which surprised her. "It's a birthday party invitation. From Claudia Severa to Sulpicia Lepidina, written around 100 CE. She's inviting her friend to a party on the eleventh, for her sister's birthday. She says she'll make the day more enjoyable by your arrival, and then it says she's sent a gift. And the closing lines are among the earliest known Latin writing by a woman."

"Their actual handwriting?" Veronica said.

"A scribe did the body of it. But the last part, the personal part, the scholars think Claudia Severa wrote that herself. Those closing lines."

Alayna had come around the table. She stood with her hand flat on the edge of it, looking down at the photograph, and her face did something Faith had never seen it do. "I wrote that they didn't exist," she said. "Women like that. I wrote that no ordinary woman in the Roman Empire left a single word, so historians just project whatever they want onto the silence. I cited it and everything."

"You can fix it," Faith said.

"Fix it how? One letter. One birthday party. I was going to say the silence was total, and now there's a woman asking her friend to come to a party on the eleventh so the day goes better." Alayna laughed, but not the way people laugh when something is funny. "It doesn't prove women were writing all over the place. It proves one woman wrote once, and the mud kept it."

The room went quiet enough that Faith could hear the radiator ticking. Outside, a boreal wind had come down early that October, stripping the maple on the lawn so completely that the branches looked drawn in pencil against the grey. Faith stared at the two maps she'd set aside, the river hopping sides between them, and something assembled itself in her head without her permission. The maps weren't lying, either of them. They were made decades apart, for different shippers, asking different questions of the same coast. And the tablet wasn't the whole truth about Roman women, but it wasn't nothing, and Alayna's silence wasn't nothing either, and both of them together were still less than what had been.

She sat down and pulled her draft toward her across the table.

"Give me your second paragraph," she said to Alayna.

"Why?"

"Because you're going to quote the invitation and then tell me it doesn't solve anything, and I'm going to tell you it solves more than you think, and one of us is going to be less wrong by Friday. I don't know which one."

"You're admitting you might be the wrong one?"

"I'm admitting the maps," Faith said. She felt the strange lightness of it, the way a confession is supposed to absolve you and mostly just leaves you standing somewhere new. Her four good paragraphs were still in her bag, still good, and she was going to take them apart anyway.

Mr. Takahashi drifted past again, glanced at the tablet lying between the two girls, and kept walking. Alayna flipped to a clean page and began copying out the Latin of the closing lines, sounding the words under her breath, and Veronica leaned over her shoulder to see what a woman's handwriting looked like after nineteen centuries in the mud.

"Happy birthday, by the way," Veronica said to no one in particular. "It's the eleventh today."

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: Early Action in US college admissions gives an early decision but is non-binding, so an admitted student may still choose not to enroll.
story:
The portal opened at five o'clock on a Thursday in December, and by fifth period Alexa still had not looked. She sat in Ms. Janssen's room with her phone face down on the desk, the radiator ticking behind her, the smell of dry-erase marker and burnt coffee settling over the empty desks around her. Wassim leaned across the aisle anyway.

"Check it," he said. "Just check it and then tell me so I can stop sweating."

"Regular Decision people don't get to sweat yet." She turned her phone over and turned it back. "You've got months."

"Yeah, but you don't." He pointed at the ceiling, at some calendar only he could see. "And if it's yes, you're done. No more essays. I would pay actual money for that."

Alexa had a spreadsheet open in her head: eleven schools left, nine essays unfinished, all due the first of January, which was sixteen days away, and she was working every weekend at the bookstore until Christmas Eve. That was the arithmetic she was carrying into the hallway when the bell rang.

She checked it in the stairwell, where the cold concrete dulled the sound of everything. Admitted. The word sat there in a small serif font, unremarkable for what it did to her knees. She read it twice, then screenshotted it, then put the phone in her pocket because a freshman was coming down the stairs and she did not want to be seen making whatever face she was making.

She found Valentina in the cafeteria line and showed her the screen without speaking. Valentina grabbed her wrist with both hands.

"Okay, so you're going," Valentina said. "That's it. You're going. I'm going to be so morose in this building without you."

"No, that's it, I'm not going, not yet." Alexa pulled the phone back. "I mean I can go. Or not. That's the whole thing with Early Action. You get the decision early, but it doesn't bind you. You can get in and still say no."

"You can?"

"That's what it is. Non-binding. I can sit on this until May and decide like everyone else."

Valentina frowned at her tray of pasta. "Then what was the point of applying early?"

"The point was knowing." Alexa realized, saying it, that knowing had a cost she hadn't bargained for. Before the stairwell she had eleven futures, all equally hypothetical. Now she had one concrete offer and ten unfinished essays, and the offer beguiled her precisely because it was finished, complete, requiring nothing further, while everything else was still work.

That afternoon she stayed after for Ms. Janssen's office hours, ostensibly to talk about her Whitman essay, which was due to her as a draft by Friday. The office smelled like the classroom, marker and coffee, and a space heater under the desk made the whole small room feel like a held breath. Ms. Janssen read the draft in silence for four minutes while Alexa sat on her hands.

"Your thesis is buried," Ms. Janssen said finally. "You've written around the thing you actually want to say. It's in the last paragraph. Cut everything above it."

"That's the admissions essay in a nutshell," Alexa said, and heard how bitter it came out, and didn't correct it.

"Something on your mind?"

Alexa laid it out like a proof on the whiteboard she was staring at. The acceptance, the nine essays, the sixteen days, the shifts at the bookstore. "So my working postulate is that an admission in hand beats a possible admission in the bush," she said. "But that assumes the other ten schools would all be worse, and I don't actually believe that. I applied to them for reasons I still think are good reasons."

Ms. Janssen tapped the draft against the desk edge. "You're asking me whether the answer changes the question."

"I'm asking whether I have to finish the applications."

"You're the only one who can answer that." She handed back the pages. "But for what it's worth, in twenty years of reading these, the students who stop the moment they get a yes are usually the ones who never really wanted the yes. They wanted the being done."

Alexa took the draft and walked out through the emptying hallway, past the trophy case, past the gym where the basketball team was already running drills and the squeak of shoes echoed off the high ceiling. She stood at her locker and opened her laptop balanced on the shelf of textbooks. The Common App tab was still there, half an essay on the screen, the cursor blinking in the middle of a sentence about her grandmother's garden.

She reread the sentence. Then she sat down on the floor with her back against the lockers, the metal cold through her jacket, and typed.

That Friday she turned in the Whitman draft with the last paragraph moved to the top, and Wassim read it over her shoulder before class.

"So you're still applying everywhere," he said.

"I'm still applying everywhere," Alexa said. She clicked submit on essay number two and watched the little green check appear next to the school's name.

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: A join with no matching condition returns every combination of rows, so 100 customers and 1,000 orders produce 100,000 rows.
story:
Sienna signed in at the front desk and carried the library's loaner laptop to the corner table by the window, where the wifi reached. She had three weeks to learn enough SQL to pass the screening for the county data internship, which paid fourteen dollars an hour, and she was impecunious in the way that made fourteen dollars an hour a fact about survival rather than a fact about wages. Amalia was already there, highlighting a biology review sheet, and Knox arrived ten minutes later with a muffin and no textbook, because Knox had finished his exam the day before and had appointed himself her tutor.

"Customers and orders," Sienna said. "Two tables. The practice problem is to find which customers ordered nothing."
