"Left join," Knox said. "You join customers to orders, keep the ones with no match, and filter for the null." He proselytized about SQL the way some people proselytize about running or a particular band, with total certainty and no interest in how he sounded.

She typed the join. The practice database loaded fast, which was the first thing that surprised her, because she had expected small and slow. One hundred customers. A thousand orders. She wrote the join and hit Enter, and the laptop stopped. The fan came up like something taking off. The screen held a spinning wheel, and rows began to fill the results pane, and kept filling, and the mouse went dead under her finger.

"What did you do," Amalia said, not looking up from her sheet.

"Nothing. I joined them. Customers to orders." The rows kept coming. She counted the counter at the bottom and watched it pass ten thousand without slowing.

Knox leaned over and read the query. "You forgot the ON," he said. "The matching condition. A join with no matching condition returns every combination of rows." He pulled the laptop toward himself, held the power button until the machine died, and handed it back. "Hundred customers, thousand orders. You asked it for a hundred thousand rows. On this thing."

Sienna rebooted and, while the screen went white and grey and rebuilt itself, wrote the numbers in her notebook. 100. 1,000. 100,000. Every combination. She had thought a join was a kind of matching, and it was, but only when you told it what to match. Without the condition it did not fail. It did everything.

By the time the desktop returned she had the corrected query half written, with the ON clause joining customer to order on customer id, and then the second problem, which was the actual problem: a customer who ordered nothing appeared in no order, so how to see what was not there. She thought of the wheel spinning, of all those rows, of the absence being invisible. She wrote LEFT JOIN, kept the customers without matches, and added WHERE the order id IS NULL. She ran it. Four names came back in under a second.

From the window table it looked different, and this is the part worth telling. Knox had known the answer before Sienna finished typing; he had, in fact, taught her the whole method, a piece of instruction that Amalia witnessed and would later confirm, though Amalia was busy with her biology and remembered it as taking less time. He watched the four names appear and felt the ordinary satisfaction of a lineage of tutors, his cousin had shown him, he showed Sienna, and so on down whatever line led back to whoever first needed to know who had ordered nothing. He did not mention that his own final project last semester had frozen the same way, on a better laptop, or that he had needed the teacher to tell him about the ON clause rather than working it out, because that detail did not fit the version of the afternoon he was already composing for the group chat. He took out his phone.

"Picture," he said. "Before you close it. Evidence for the archive."

Sienna moved her water bottle out of the frame and let him photograph the screen with its four names. She looked at them a while longer after the phone went down. One of the names was Marisol Trent, whom she did not know, a person who existed in this county, had a customer id, and had ordered nothing at all. Somewhere there was a reason, but the query did not carry reasons. It carried rows, and the absence of rows, and she understood that she had learned to ask a narrow question exactly and that everything else about Marisol Trent stayed where it had always been, outside the tables.

Ms. Zhu came by on her rounds, checked the laptop's temperature with the back of her hand, and said, "This machine is due back at six."

"We're done," Sienna said. She saved her file twice, closed the laptop, and wrote one more line in her notebook under the 100,000: which customers ordered nothing. Then she copied the four names onto the next page, in ink, and put the notebook in her bag.

Amalia looked up. "So do you actually know this now, or do you know it the way Knox knows things?"

"Ask me Thursday," Sienna said, and carried the laptop back to the desk.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Before the Eid al-Fitr prayer, Muslims who can afford it give a set charity called zakat al-fitr for each family member, so that poor families can also celebrate Eid.
story:
The cultural center smelled of cardamom and floor polish, and Logan's father stood at the folding table by the prayer hall doors counting envelopes into a shoebox. Logan had come because his mother had said the words "your father needs help" in the tone she reserved for things not open to negotiation, and now he was holding a list of names in his own handwriting while his father handled the money.

"Seven," his father said. "One for each of us." He laid out the envelopes in a row like dominoes. "This is zakat al-fitr. Before the Eid prayer tomorrow, every Muslim who can afford it gives a set amount for each person in the household, so that poor families can celebrate Eid too."

Logan wrote the number seven at the top of the list. In his head he was already doing what he always did, which was to run the thing through the machinery of his economics elective, where Mr. Chen had taught them to amortize a cost across a whole system and see who actually ended up paying it. Spreading a fixed obligation across everyone who could bear it, so that the burden landed nowhere too heavily and the benefit landed everywhere. It was elegant. It was, he thought, the kind of design a committee of very smart people would take months to reach, except it had been running for over a thousand years without a whiteboard.

His friend Rogan appeared from the direction of the kitchen carrying a tray of dates and found Logan at the table. Rogan's family had been coming to this center since before either of them could walk, and Rogan himself wanted, more than anything this year, to be asked to lead the youth recitation at tomorrow's prayer, a job usually given to a college student. He set the dates down and leaned in.

"You're doing the zakat?" Rogan said. "My dad made me do ours last year. I messed it up, forgot my grandmother counts, she lives with us."

"So it's per person," Logan said, mostly to himself. "Not per family."

"Per person," his father confirmed, without looking up. "Everyone who can afford it. A set charity, the same set amount, before the prayer." He squared the envelopes against the table's edge with two taps.

Logan had brought a second thought with him, the one he'd been arguing in his head since the car ride over. His father worked two jobs and their rent had gone up in the spring, and Logan had done the arithmetic: his own share could cover the textbook deposit he'd need in September. He believed in the logic of the system; he also believed in the logic of his own situation, and the two logics were standing on the same small envelope.

He turned the problem over the way Mr. Chen had taught them to turn over the idea of an oligarchy, a few hands holding what many needed. If everyone who could pay decided their own need was special, the poor families the charity existed for would end up with nothing on the one morning a year the whole point was that no one should have nothing. His situation was real. It was also, he had to admit, not that situation. He had textbooks coming. Someone else had an empty table coming.

Still, he didn't like the parsimonious little voice in his head that had already drafted the argument for keeping the money, the one that dressed up keeping as prudence. His grandmother, who was sitting on a chair near the entrance watching the volunteers string lights, had once told him that the fastest way to ruin a good idea was to decide you were its exception.

"I was thinking," Logan said to his father, "that I might cover my own out of my savings. The deposit can wait a month."

His father looked up then, and for a second Logan saw him doing his own arithmetic, the kind parents do about what a child has understood and when. "If you're sure," his father said.

"I'm sure. It's per person anyway. Might as well actually be per person."

Rogan had drifted toward the stage, where the center's director was taping up the order of events for tomorrow, and Logan watched him hover there with the empty date tray until the director noticed him and said something that made Rogan straighten up and point at himself, twice, as if to make sure they were both talking about the same person.

His father slid one envelope out of the row and set it in front of Logan, unsealed, empty. "Then fill this one yourself," he said, and went back to his count.

Logan took the bills from his wallet, the ones earmarked for the deposit, and slid them in one at a time. Across the hall, the lights his grandmother had been watching flickered on all at once, and the whole ceiling of the prayer hall turned gold.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: In the United States, a new employee fills out Form W-4 so the employer knows how much federal income tax to withhold from each paycheck.
story:
The hardware store smelled of cut pine and machine oil, and Ava stood at the register counter filling out paperwork instead of buying anything, which felt like a form of trespass. Ms. Sultani, the owner, had shaken her hand twenty minutes earlier and said welcome aboard, a phrase Ava had previously heard only in movies about ships. Now she was alone with a clipboard, a pen on a bead chain, and a form she had never seen before.

"Form W-4," Alvin had said that morning, when she told him she'd gotten the job. He worked at the grocery store across the lot and spoke about employment with the weary authority of a man twice his age. "Wait till you get to the W-4. It humbles you." Ava had assumed he was joking. Alvin joked about most things, especially the ones that had quietly frightened him.

The form wanted things she knew: name, address, Social Security number, which she recited from memory in her mother's voice. Then it wanted allowances and withholding, words that sat on the page like furniture in a dark room. She understood from the shape of the top line, Employee's Withholding Certificate, that the form was about money, and that the money in question was not the eight dollars an hour she'd negotiated but some portion of it that would leave before the rest reached her.

She took out her phone and texted her mother: what is a w-4. The response came in three parts, because her mother's thumbs worked in paragraphs. A new employee fills out Form W-4, the first message said, so the employer knows how much federal income tax to withhold from each paycheck. The second message said ask Ms. Sultani if you're stuck, don't guess. The third was a thumbs up, which Ava understood to mean the conversation was over.

A second voice arrived at her shoulder. Anaelle, who had been restocking paintbrushes in aisle four and had the dust of the substrate boards on her sleeves to prove it, leaned over the clipboard. "You look like the form insulted you," she said.

"It kind of did. It's asking me to decide things about taxes. I'm eighteen. I voted for the first time three weeks ago and I still don't know where the polling place was."

"That's the spirit," Anaelle said. "I put myself as single, one job, and the boxes didn't argue with me. That's the whole trick as far as I know." She wandered back toward the brushes, apparently satisfied that this constituted training.

Ava looked at the form again. Her mother's sentence had rearranged something in her head. It wasn't a test with a right answer, it was a message to her employer: this is what I'm telling you about myself, and you use it to take out the right amount. Whatever the mechanics were beyond that, the form existed so that someone with a payroll system would know how much to withhold. She checked the single box. She checked one job. She wrote her name again at the bottom, and her signature looked strange, half-familiar, like a photograph of herself taken from an angle she didn't usually see.

She carried the clipboard to the back office, where Ms. Sultani was arguing with a distributor about a shipment of galvanized screws. "Done," Ava said, setting it on the desk.

Ms. Sultani held the form up to the light, an inspection ritual that seemed to aggrandize a single sheet of paper into a matter of state. "Good. Now you're official. Which means," she said, and paused long enough that Ava braced for a speech about responsibility, "you can official unload that truck of mulch before it blocks the fire lane."

The mulch was outside in the sun, forty bags of it stacked on pallets by the lumber, and the work was exactly as unromantic as she'd been promised it would be. Somewhere in the middle of the stack she stopped caring about taxes, forms, the strange adulthood of it all, and cared only about grip and leverage and the littoral zone of shade at the edge of the building, where she set each bag before ferrying it inside. Alvin crossed the lot on his break and stood watching her lift.

"So it humbled you," he called.

"It was fine, actually. It's just a form that tells them how much to take out. You made it sound like a trial."

"I like to aggrandize my suffering," Alvin said. "It's all I have."

She carried the next bag past him without answering, and the receipt paper of her first hour of work, which Ms. Sultani had folded into her pocket as a joke, crinkled there like a promise.

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: Payment history is the largest factor in a FICO credit score, making up about 35 percent of it for the general population.
story:
The phone store smelled like new plastic and floor cleaner, and Emile stood in front of the display case knowing exactly which phone he wanted, the one with the midnight finish that lay flat against the glass like a sheet of black water. He had seventy dollars in his savings account and a job at the garden center that paid him every other Friday, which was enough to be dangerous. The saleswoman asked if he wanted to finance it, twenty-four months, no money down, and when he asked what that meant she drew a little schedule on a brochure. The phone cost eight hundred forty dollars. Financed, it would cost nine hundred twelve, because the money was borrowed and borrowed money gathered interest the way a snowball gathers snow, a few dollars a month, quiet and relentless.

"Or," said Maliyah, who was there because her charger had frayed, "you save up and buy it outright, and the interest works for you instead. My account pays me like two percent. It's not much, but it goes the other direction." She said this with the gravitas of someone who had recently discovered compound interest and mentioned it in approximately every conversation, including the one at lunch about the cafeteria's new fries.

Emile said he'd think about it, but what he was actually thinking about was the bill. Two months ago he had forgotten his share of the family phone plan, thirty-eight dollars, and his father had covered it and Emile had paid him back in cash, but somewhere in the shuffle the carrier had recorded a late payment. He'd gotten an email about it and deleted it, the way you delete something hoping it deletes the fact too.

Peter was leaning on the counter, reading the brochure upside down. "You're going to check your score, aren't you," he said. It wasn't a question. Peter had a checking app and the doctrinaire certainty of someone who had read one article about personal finance and decided that everyone else was reckless. "You can look it up free. It's a FICO score."

"I know what it is."

"You know what it's called. You don't know what's in it." Peter unlocked his phone and handed it over like a man presenting evidence. On the screen was a breakdown with colored bars. Payment history stretched across the top, longer than anything else. Emile tapped it and read the line twice. Payment history is the largest factor in a FICO score, making up about 35 percent of it.

"Thirty-five percent," Emile said out loud.

"For most people, yeah." Peter took the phone back. Emile wanted to vilify him for being right, for the small satisfied way he pocketed the phone, but the numbers were the numbers and Peter hadn't invented them. Emile pulled up his own report on his cracked old phone, the one whose screen had a hairline fracture running through the middle of everything like a river on a map. The late payment sat there in plain type. His score was six hundred eighty-one. It didn't say how much the late payment had cost him, whether he'd have been seven hundred without it or seven hundred forty, and nothing on the screen would tell him. The number was a verdict with no reasoning attached.

He thought about the snowball again. Interest going the wrong way on nine hundred twelve dollars, and payment history going the wrong way on thirty-eight, and both of them doing their quiet work whether he watched or not. It would have been easy to decide, in that moment, that credit was a trap laid by people in suits, except that Maliyah's savings account was the same mechanism pointed the other direction, and the saleswoman had been perfectly pleasant, and the whole thing was less a villain than a kind of weather. He didn't like the weather. He just had to walk around in it.

"The refurbished one," he said finally, pointing at the case. It was the same phone, a year older, six hundred fifty dollars all at once. The saleswoman began the paperwork. Maliyah said "smart" in the tone of someone awarding a medal, and Emile felt both pleased and poorer, the two feelings arriving together like passengers sharing a cab. He would keep his savings, mostly, minus a hundred fifty he didn't have yet, and he would owe his father, and the late payment would sit on his report for years doing whatever it did.

Outside, the afternoon had gone gold and the parking lot smelled of hot asphalt. Maliyah peeled off toward the bus stop, and Peter clapped him once on the shoulder. "Set up autopay," Peter said, already crossing the lot. "Then you never think about it again." Emile stood holding the bag with the refurbished box inside it, lighter than he expected, and texted his father: I'll pay you back Friday, with interest.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: All 50 US states and Washington, DC allow minors to consent to testing and treatment for sexually transmitted infections without a parent's permission, though some states set a minimum age.
story:
The second-floor bathroom smelled of disinfectant and someone's mango shampoo, and Isabelle had claimed the far corner by the window because it was the only place in the building where she could spread her note cards on the sill without a lunch table's audience. She was rehearsing. In forty hours she would stand in front of Mr. Mendoza's ninth-grade health class, two years younger than her, and explain consent, contraception, and where to get tested, because the school's actual health teacher had flatly refused and Mr. Mendoza had said, with a shrug that Isabelle still found astonishing, "You wrote the proposal. You should give the talk."

"You're doing it out loud," Evie said from the sink, where she was refilling her water bottle without looking at it. "You know that, right."

"That's the point." Isabelle squared the cards. "If I can't say it to you, in a bathroom, I can't say it to thirty fourteen-year-olds."

Evie came over, drying her hands on her jeans, and picked up the top card, the one that said CONSENT in Isabelle's cramped capitals. She read it in silence, and something in her face closed like a door easing shut, not slammed.

"Ask me," Isabelle said.

"It's fine. It's good. You have like, definitions and everything."

"Evie. Ask me the thing you actually want to ask."

The hand dryer in the corner started up on its own, the way it did, roaring at nobody. They both waited it out. When it died, Evie set the card down with exaggerated care, the way you handle something that might be hotter than it looks.

"If somebody wanted to get tested," she said, "at a clinic. Like the one on Delancey Street. They'd need a parent to sign something, wouldn't they. A permission form, like for the field trip."

Isabelle opened her mouth to say yes, because that was her instinct too, and then stopped, because she had spent three weeks buried in this and instinct was not what the three weeks were for. "No," she said, slowly, testing the word. "They don't. I kept thinking they did, and I kept looking for the form, and there isn't one. All fifty states and DC let minors consent to testing and treatment for infections themselves. Without a parent."

Evie's shoulders came down maybe half an inch. "Everywhere? Like even here?"

"Everywhere. Some states set a minimum age, so you'd want to check yours, but there's no parental signature. Not for that." She pulled the card with the clinic's address from the middle of the stack and held it out. "That's the whole reason I put this slide in. Because everyone thinks there's a form."

Evie took the card and looked at the address as if it might change under her eyes. "Lauriane went there in October," she said. "She told you, right? She told me she was going to tell you."

"She told me she had a dentist appointment and then was weirdly effusive about my haircut for like ten minutes."

"That's her. That's her telling you." Evie laughed once, not much of a laugh. "She said the nurse just talked to her, one on one. She said it was, like, boring. Paperwork and a swab. She was in and out before her mom thought she'd been at the dentist."

The late bell for fifth period rang somewhere below them, distant and formal, and neither of them moved. Isabelle watched Evie fold the card in half, then unfold it, then fold it again along the same crease, as though repetition could make it smaller to carry.

"You could go with her," Isabelle said. "Thursday afternoon. She told me the clinic does walk-ins till five."

"I don't need to go, I just." Evie stopped. Started again, quieter. "There's this guy. From the tournament in March. And I keep not thinking about it, and then I think about it, and it's been since March, Isabelle."

"Then Thursday." Isabelle slid the note cards together and squared them against the sill. "And I'll come too, if you want. I'll bring homework and be an epicure of the vending machine and sit in the lobby being absolutely no help whatsoever."

"You'd do that."

"Obviously I'd do that." She said it lightly, because the light version was what Evie could accept right now, and Isabelle had learned, somewhere in these three weeks of drafting and redrafting, that the heavy version of a true thing can land like a hand pressed on a bruise. Consent, she had written on the first card, is ongoing and enthusiastic and can be withdrawn, and she had been thinking about sex when she wrote it, mostly, but the words kept applying themselves to other things. To a friend folding a card. To the space you leave around a person who is deciding something hard.

"There's one thing I haven't figured out," she admitted, and it cost her something to say it, after all the competence of the last ten minutes. "For the ninth graders. I have the law, and I have the clinic, and I have all of it down cold. But I don't know how to say the part where you're scared to walk in the door. Mr. Mendoza says just give them the facts. But the facts aren't why people don't go."

Evie tucked the card into the back pocket of her jeans, smoothing it flat with her palm. "Tell them about the vending machine," she said. "Tell them somebody will sit in the lobby."

She shouldered her bag and pushed open the bathroom door, and Isabelle stood a moment longer at the window, looking down at the parking lot, at the space where the number 17 bus turned around, the one that went to Delancey Street.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Spike tape is coloured tape used to mark where furniture and actors should be placed on the stage floor.
story:
The gym smelled of varnish and cold coffee, and Ashton had until Friday to make a one-act out of nine pages and two actors who did not like each other. He had been given the slot because the senior directors had all graduated, which meant nobody was left who knew anything, and Ms. Tesfaye had said, "You'll figure it out," in the tone people use when they have decided not to help. He stood at the folding table that served as his desk and watched Brogan and Maelie run the second scene for the fourth time, and for the fourth time the sofa they had borrowed from the drama room ended up somewhere it should not be.

The blocking was simple, or it was supposed to be. Maelie sat on the sofa, Brogan crossed to her, they argued, he left. But Brogan crossed at a different angle every run, and Maelie, who could not see the room from where she sat, kept turning her body to face wherever he happened to be, so that by the end of the scene she was practically in the aisle. "You're drifting," Ashton called, and Brogan said, "I'm acting," and Maelie said nothing, which was how she disagreed with things.

At rehearsal on Wednesday he tried taping an X on the floor with masking tape he'd found in the janitor's closet. It peeled by the second run, a grey curl that Brogan stepped on and dragged a foot away. The sofa itself was worse, because whoever pushed it back into place after each scene pushed it somewhere slightly different, and the whole geometry of the argument changed depending on whether Maelie was near the door or near the bleachers. Ashton had read somewhere that theatre was a visual art and had believed it in an abstract way. He was now learning it as a fact about furniture.

He went to Ms. Tesfaye during her free period and asked whether there was such a thing as tape that stayed down on gym floors. She said there was a box in the drama room, second shelf, and that he should look for the colours. The box held rolls of narrow tape in fluorescent pink, yellow, and green, and a label in someone's handwriting that read spike tape. He took the pink and the green and read the label twice on the way back, because the word was new and he did not want to use it wrong in front of people who would notice.

That evening he laid the tape out before anyone arrived. A pink T where the sofa's front legs belonged, a green X where Brogan was to end his cross. When Maelie came in she looked at the marks and said, "What's that for?"

"It's called spike tape," Ashton said. "It marks where furniture and actors go."

She crouched and pressed the edge of the green X flat with her thumb. "So I can see where he's supposed to be without turning my head."

"Exactly."

The next run was different, and not only because things stopped drifting. Maelie, freed from tracking Brogan's wanderings, sat still and let him come to her, and the stillness read as something Ashton had not planned, a refusal to chase the argument. Brogan hit his mark and found himself close enough that his last line had to be quieter than he wanted, and the quiet worked. Afterwards Ashton stood in the aisle with his script and did not write anything down, because the thing that had happened was not on the page. He had spent two weeks thinking his job was to decide where people went, and now he suspected it was something closer to building conditions and then getting out of the way, though he could not have said where one ended and the other began, and he did not fully trust the suspicion either. Some of what happened in a room was just the room.

Brogan had his own theory, offered while winding the pink roll back up. "The tape is like a ritual," he said. "Football players do the same warm-up every game. It's not superstition, it's how you tell your body where it is."

"That's not what it is," Maelie said.

"It could be both."

Ashton said, "It's tape." But walking out through the lobby afterward he found himself historicizing the whole business, thinking about how every stage he had ever seen must have had marks under the paint, how the practice went back further than he could trace, and how strange it was that the trace was meant to be invisible. He thought about the phenomenology of it only briefly and without the word, and then with the word, which he had learned in a class he was taking for credit he didn't need: the way a small square of green changed what a body knew about a space, without the body being told anything. The masking tape X he had first tried was already vestigial in his memory, a version of himself that had thought any adhesive would do.

On Friday they performed in the gym with the bleachers pulled out halfway and forty folding chairs in rows. The sofa hit its mark every time. The marks themselves disappeared under the lights, as they were supposed to, and only Ashton, standing at the back by the water fountain, knew exactly where they were. When Brogan crossed to the green X and stopped a foot from Maelie's knees, Ashton watched the audience lean forward in one motion, like a field of grass. After the lights came up, Ms. Tesfaye found him coiling the pink tape around his hand.

"Keep the box," she said. "You'll want it next year."

"I don't know if I'm doing this next year."

She looked at the empty stage, then at him. "The floor's marked either way," she said, and walked off toward the doors.

activity: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
knowledge_domain: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
fact: In 1904 physicist Robert W. Wood secretly removed a key prism from René Blondlot's apparatus, yet observers still reported seeing Blondlot's claimed 'N-rays', showing they were seeing what they expected.
story:
The bus from Riverside High let them off outside the physics building at nine, and by nine fifteen Makayla was already losing the argument. Ms. Perera had paired her with Elodie for the diffusion lab, and Elodie was certain the interference rings looked sharper on the second run.

"Look at that edge," Elodie said, leaning over the optical bench. "That's cleaner than run one. The slit width is doing exactly what the manual said it would."

"It's doing what the manual said you'd see," Makayla said. She wrote "run 2" in the notebook and did not write "sharper." Elodie read the setup sheet before every run. Makayla had watched her do it, had watched her hand hover over the paragraph titled Expected Pattern before she put her eye to the screen.

Caitlyn drifted over from the next bench, gloved hands held up like a surgeon. "You two are still fighting about fringes?"

"She won't count what she sees," Elodie said.

"She counts what she sees after she's read what she's supposed to see."

Down the corridor, past the liquid nitrogen cart, there was a small exhibit case the class was meant to visit after lunch: a brass prism on velvet, a photograph of a laboratory from before the first war. Makayla finished the data table early and went to look at it, mostly to be away from the bench. Caitlyn followed.

The card beside the prism was short. It described a French physicist named René Blondlot who had announced the discovery of what he called N-rays. It described Robert W. Wood, a physicist who, in 1904, went to Blondlot's lab, and while the apparatus was running, secretly removed a key prism from it. The observers still reported seeing the N-rays. The card said the demonstration helped show why replication matters.

"Wait," Caitlyn said, reading over her shoulder. "He took the prism out, and they still saw them?"

"With their eyes open," Makayla said. "Reporting measurements."

"That's horrifying."

Makayla copied the date into her notebook, then the two names, then stood looking at the velvet. She was thinking about Elodie's certainty, and about her own certainty that Elodie was wrong, and about the fact that both of them had looked at the same screen. She turned the problem over the way she'd been taught to turn a proof: what evidence would settle it, and who would have to gather it.

Back in the lab, she found Ms. Perera checking the helium neon laser on bench four and asked whether the class could repeat a run without the setup sheet. Ms. Perera said the sheets had to stay with the benches, so Makayla proposed it differently: let Elodie run the diffraction grating blind, covers on the setup parameters, parameters chosen by someone else.

"You want to blind your own partner," Ms. Perera said.

"I want her to be right for the right reason. If the rings are sharper, they'll be sharper whether she reads the sheet or not."

Ms. Perera looked at her for a moment, then at the bench. "Caitlyn sets the slit width and doesn't tell either of you. You record the images. Swap the parameters between runs and keep the key with me until you've counted the fringes."

They ran it after lunch. Caitlyn set the slits behind a cardboard screen and logged the settings on a folded paper she handed to Ms. Perera, who pocketed it without looking. Elodie put her eye to the screen four times, and each time Makayla counted fringes first, calling out only "recorded," before Elodie gave her judgment. It was slow and awkward and the second run had to be redone because someone knocked the mount.

When they unfolded the key at the end, Elodie had called two of the narrow-slit runs "sharper" and two of the wide-slit runs "sharper." Under blind conditions her judgments tracked nothing. She read the tally twice, her thumb pressing the paper flat.

"So it was the sheet," she said.

"We don't know that," Makayla said. "It's four runs. It could be me counting wrong, it could be the screen. We'd need to do it a lot more times, and have other people do it, before anyone could say."

"That's not a very satisfying answer."

"No," Makayla agreed. "But it's tenable."

Later, on the bus, Caitlyn exhumed the folded key from the bottom of her bag, smoothed it on the seat between them, and said, "Run three was your favorite. Wide slit."

Elodie leaned across the aisle and looked at the numbers a long time. "Do it again Monday," she said. "And I don't read anything first."

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: Canada's Rand formula, from Justice Ivan Rand's 1946 ruling after a Ford strike in Windsor, Ontario, requires all workers covered by a union contract to pay dues.
story:
The first paycheck came in a thin envelope that smelled of cardboard and toner, and Lea read it twice under the buzzing fluorescents of the warehouse lunchroom before she understood what was missing. Nine dollars an hour, thirty-one hours, and then a line she hadn't expected: union dues, eleven dollars and change, gone before the money ever touched her hands. She had signed a stack of forms on her first day. Apparently one of them had signed her into something she'd never agreed to join.

"Did you sign up for the union?" she asked Drake, who was eating noodles out of a container balanced on a pallet jack. The loading bay door behind him was rolled up to the August heat, and somewhere out in the yard a truck was backing up, beeping in a slow, patient rhythm.

"Never signed anything," Drake said. "Doesn't matter. It comes off anyway."

"That's theft." She said it half as a joke, but the number on the stub had already begun to bother her. Eleven dollars was a movie and a bus fare. Eleven dollars, every two weeks, was her mother's phone bill at the end of a summer.

Drake shrugged with his whole body, the way he did when he'd decided a conversation wasn't worth its weight. "Ask Tabitha. Her cousin works at the Ford plant. Or ask Mr. Rosen. He's the steward." He tilted his head toward the far corner, where a man with grey stubble and a clipboard was taping a notice to the corkboard by the time clock. The notice was about overtime, something about the company wanting Sunday shifts and the union filing a grievance. Lea had walked past it every day for two weeks without reading a word.

She read it now, while Mr. Rosen pressed down the last corner of tape. "I never joined the union," she said, quieter than she meant to. "Why am I paying dues?"

Mr. Rosen looked at her for a second, and she braced herself for a speech, the kind adults gave when they thought you were too young to have asked the question. Instead he said, "How old are you?" and when she told him, he nodded slowly and said, "You'll pay them either way. Everybody covered by the contract pays. Ask Tabitha about the Rand formula. It came out of a strike at Ford in Windsor." Then he picked up his clipboard and walked off toward the aisles, and she was left holding half an answer.

Tabitha was on the evening shift, so Lea waited until the dock went quiet, the last trailer sealed and the forklifts charging in their bays with a sound like distant rain. She found Tabitha refilling her water bottle by the bathrooms, and Tabitha told it the way her cousin had told her: after the Ford strike in Windsor, Ontario, back in 1946, Justice Ivan Rand ruled that all the workers covered by a union contract had to pay dues, whether they'd signed up or not. "My cousin calls it paying your share," Tabitha said, screwing the cap back on. "Everybody gets the raise the union bargains for. So everybody pays." She didn't say it like a lesson. She said it like a fact she'd once resented and then stopped resenting, and Lea couldn't tell which part had changed, her or the math.

Sitting on the loading dock afterward with her legs hanging over the edge, Lea counted it out on her fingers like a child. Eleven dollars out. But the notice on the corkboard was about Sunday overtime, and the schedule taped beside it capped her at forty hours, and when the temp agency girl in receiving had been sent home early three shifts running, someone had called Mr. Rosen and it had stopped. Her mother had worked an office job two summers ago with none of that, no contract, no steward, just a manager who said take it or leave it. Maybe that was the trade, the way her grandmother talked about her annuity, money leaving now so that something would hold later, though the comparison felt equivocal at best, half borrowed, since she couldn't yet say what the union's promises were worth in her hands. She only knew she'd walked in wanting her eleven dollars back, and she was walking out not sure anymore whether the stub had been shorting her or telling her something. Behind her the yard lights clicked on all at once, and Drake pushed through the door with his noodle container, saying, "You still mad about your check?"

"I don't know yet," Lea said, folding the stub into her back pocket.

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: Under English common law, consideration must have some value but need not be a fair price; courts do not generally judge whether a bargain was a good one.
story:
The bank smelled of carpet cleaner and cold air, and the queue moved in the slow way queues do on Saturday mornings. Carter held the folded twenty-pound note in his fist so tightly that the Queen's face had gone soft along the crease. When his turn came, the teller slid a form across the counter and asked him to read the terms and conditions printed on the back before signing. He read them. Liability for losses, consent to share information with third parties, a signature block at the bottom waiting for him in pale blue lines. He had never signed anything before except a school trip form and the register, and the pen felt heavier than a pen should.

The twenty pounds had come from Isobel, yesterday, outside the leisure centre. She had been saving for a festival ticket all summer and was still short, and the ticket had dropped in price that morning, a synchronicity she described with both hands raised, as if the universe had arranged it. She needed a bike to get to her weekend job at the garden centre, starting in two weeks. Carter's bike, the one his uncle had rebuilt with him the spring before he died, was worth three hundred easily; he had checked the listings. Isobel had twenty pounds left after the ticket. He had looked at her face and said fine, take it, and she had counted the note into his hand with the solemnity of someone closing a mortgage.

He had regretted it within the hour, and by evening the regret had settled into something more turbid, a mixture he couldn't separate into grief for the bike and shame at wanting it back. He had texted Isobel at midnight and again at seven. She had replied only: come to the bank at ten, I'm opening an account too, we'll talk.

Mr. Cohen was already there, standing at the counter with a bag of coins, a retired solicitor who lived three doors down and who had once, years ago, spoken at Carter's school about how contracts were everywhere, in bus tickets and haircuts and promises made in playgrounds. Carter remembered being nine years old in that assembly, enthralled by the idea that words could bind you, that saying yes was a kind of glue. He remembered going home and making his mother sign a slip of paper promising fish and chips on Friday, and how she had honoured it, laughing, even when the money was short.

Isobel was sitting in the waiting area filling in her own form, printing her details in careful capitals. "I'll give the bike back," she said before he could sit down. "I didn't sleep either. But I want to know first whether I have to, or whether I'm just being decent. There's a difference." She held up her phone. "My sister's first-year law textbook. Look."

Carter read the screen. The section said that under English common law, consideration, meaning whatever each side gives up in a bargain, must have some value, but it need not be a fair price. Courts did not generally judge whether a bargain was a good one.

"So a peppercorn counts," Isobel said. "That's the word they use. A peppercorn."

"A peppercorn," Carter repeated. It felt strange in his mouth, a word for a deal so lopsided it had become law-school shorthand. Twenty pounds for a three-hundred-pound bike was not a peppercorn exactly, but it stood on the same principle: the value existed, the exchange was real, and no court would weigh whether he had been cheated.

"I thought there'd be some rule," he said. "Like, if it's obviously unfair, you can undo it."

"Apparently not, generally. A bargain's a bargain."

"It's not her fault," Carter said, and was surprised that he meant it as a defence of the deal rather than of himself. He thought of Mr. Cohen's assembly again, the idea that consent given freely was the glue, and set it against the other idea, the one his mother lived by, that some deals shouldn't be allowed to stand no matter who nodded. Both felt true. He could not make them sit together neatly, and he decided he didn't have to, not here, not at ten in the morning in a bank that smelled of carpet cleaner.

He went to the counter, handed over the twenty, and signed the form under the line marked signature, his name suddenly formal in his own handwriting. The teller stamped something and welcomed him as a customer of the bank, and the account, apparently, was now open, its terms binding.

Carter walked back to the waiting area and sat down beside Isobel. "Keep the bike," he said. "But you're paying for the bus to the festival, and I get first refusal if you ever sell it."

"Those are my terms and conditions," Isobel said, and smiled, and shook his hand across the armrest of the chair.

The scene two collision happened on Tuesday, and by Wednesday Victor had the tape measure out in the community theatre basement before anyone else arrived. Liana and Diya had been crossing upstage left at the same moment, Liana carrying an imaginary tray, Diya turning to deliver her monologue, and the two of them had clipped shoulders so hard that Diya dropped her script pages into the fan. Mr. Weber, who ran the drama camp and had given Victor the one-act to direct, had watched from the folding chairs and said only, "You might want to settle that before Friday."

Victor knelt on the boards with a pencil and a roll of blue masking tape. He had read the chapter in the directing book twice on the bus, the one that said blocking is the planned positioning and movement of actors on stage, set by the director during rehearsals. He had underlined it and then felt slightly foolish for underlining a definition. Still, the definition was doing something to him. He had thought directing meant having opinions about the lines. Now it seemed to mean deciding where bodies were, and when, and why, before anyone spoke.

When Liana came in with her coffee, he was taping a small X near the prop table. "What's that?" she said.

"Where you put the tray down," Victor said. "Then you cross downstage right while Diya's still talking, and she turns on this spot here."

Liana looked at the tape, then at him. "So you've decided where I go."

"I've decided where the scene goes. Or I'm trying."

She set her coffee down outside the taped area, deliberately, he thought, the way she did things deliberately. Last year she had directed the winter showcase and Victor had acted in it, badly, and they both remembered that. There was a version of this where she took his tape marks as a demotion, and a version where she took them as relief, and he could not tell from her face which one she was standing in.

Diya arrived at four with her pages re-stapled. They ran scene two. The crossings worked; nobody collided; the tray found its X. But the monologue went flat, and Victor knew it before Diya finished. She stood exactly where he had taped her and delivered eleven lines without moving her feet, as though the tape were glue rather than a place to pass through. He stopped the run.

"That's not what the tape means," he said. "It's a place, not a prison."

"Then what is it for?" Diya said. She was not being difficult. She actually wanted to know, and he found he had to find out too, out loud, in front of them.

He thought of his father, who laid out garden beds with string and never once explained a single plant. The string delimited the bed; the growing was left to the thing growing. Maybe tape was like that. "It delimits where the audience looks," he said. "What you do inside it is yours."

Liana crossed her arms. "That's sophistry. You either want us where you put us or you don't."

She was partly right, and he made himself say so, because the alternative was pretending a neat answer existed. "I want you where I put you at the moments that matter. The rest I want you to find. I don't know yet which moments are which. That's the honest version."

They ran it again. Diya kept her mark for the first three lines and then, on the fourth, drifted half a step toward Liana, and the drift did something to the line, gave it an address, a person it was aimed at. Victor felt the change in the room the way you feel a door open somewhere in a house. He wrote in the margin of his script: keep the drift. Then he crossed it out and wrote: let her drift. The difference between those two notes seemed suddenly like the whole problem of directing, maybe of other things too, though he didn't chase that thought any further.

Mr. Weber came down at five and sat in the back row without asking. They ran scene two all the way through, then scene one, then scene two again. At the second run, Liana set the tray down a foot from the X, outside it, and looked at Victor over her shoulder. He let it stand. The tray read better there, catching the work light.

Afterward Mr. Weber said nothing about the tray. He said, "Friday, seven o'clock, and don't let them phone it in," and went back upstairs. His restraint felt like a grade he hadn't been shown yet.

The girls gathered their bags. Diya paused at the door with her stapled pages. "Same tape tomorrow?"

"Same tape," Victor said. He was already peeling up the X by the prop table and pressing down a new one, a few inches north, for no reason he could defend and no reason he wanted to. Liana watched him do it from the doorway, drinking the last of her coffee, and said, "You know that's worse."
